articles.title: India: Online censorship grows after 'Cockroach' protests
articles.summary: Since anti-government Cockroach protests erupted, journalists and creators say their content is increasingly being restricted on social media in India.

image.caption: Digital restrictions have affected independent content creators, journalists and established media organizations, raising concerns about online free speech [FILE: April 2, 2026]Image: Sandeep Singh

blocks.text: A video showing a young girl crying as she spoke about alleged police brutality during the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in July. A video examining the Hindu nationalist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh's (RSS) contribution to the rise of India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). A satirical cartoon criticizing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
These are among the examples of content that have recently been restricted on social media in India.
A pattern of restrictions
Content creator CitySavitri describes herself as a "nobody" in the world of social media. She had started making videos just two months ago and had around 600 followers on Instagram.
Yet a video looking at the RSS's role in the BJP's 2014 election victory was restricted in India within an hour of being posted. It was the first of three videos she posted that faced restrictions.
The experience made her feel that "anti-government commentary" was being monitored and curtailed.
"It is very plain and simple to understand," the content creator told DW.
Independent journalist Sadhika Tiwari was covering the CJP protest in New Delhi on July 20, when police used batons and tear gas against demonstrators.
Tiwari's video of a frightened young girl crying and speaking about police brutality garnered around 10 million views within hours, she said, before it was restricted in India.
Political cartoonist Satish Acharya has also faced repeated restrictions, with Instagram blocking his profile twice recently.
'Suppressing independent journalism'

In May 2025, during the conflict between India and Pakistan, independent digital news outlet Maktoob Media's X account was withheld in India while it was reporting on the escalating crisis, its founder and editor Aslah Kayyalakkath told DW.
"We received no official notice or email from either the government or X. It was our readers who first alerted us to the blocking," he said.
Maktoob Media said it contacted Indian officials and X but received no response. Access to the account was restored a few days later, again without an explanation.
Kayyalakkath said Maktoob's content from the July protest also faced restrictions. "Suppressing independent journalism undermines transparency, accountability and democratic values," he said.
Several of the content creators and journalists interviewed by DW said they received no prior notification or explanation for the restrictions.
Some users were not sure if their content had been blocked at the government's request or proactively by the social media platforms.
When asked for comment, Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, pointed DW to a website statement noting users can appeal content and account restrictions.
How does the system work?

At the heart of the debate are India's IT Rules, 2021, amended in February 2026. Section 79 of India's IT Act protects social media platforms and other intermediaries from liability for content posted by third parties, provided they meet certain legal conditions.

One such requirement, introduced through the February 2026 amendments, is to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content within three hours of receiving a valid court order or a reasoned government notice. The previous deadline was 36 hours.
Failure to comply can result in intermediaries losing their liability protection.
Censorship in India: Muzzled by the government
The government's Sahyog portal, which coordinates takedown requests between law enforcement, platforms and telecom providers, has faced criticism over the pace at which notices are issued.

Meta said it uses automated tools and technologies to detect and review content that may violate its community standards. It also automatically restricts access to certain types of content in India to comply with legal requirements under the IT rules.

Pranesh Prakash, a technology law and policy adviser, said the amended rules allow authorized police officials to notify intermediaries about content they consider unlawful without necessarily filing a formal complaint or initiating other legal proceedings.

"This has led to the worst period of social media censorship that India has ever seen, with digital news media accounts being blocked, cartoonists' accounts being blocked, and even mere discussions of an opposition leader's memoirs being blocked," he said. "Clearly, none of these disclosed any 'unlawful acts.'"
Prakash also raised concerns about the lack of public information on government requests to remove content, saying this made it difficult to assess the scale of restrictions.
A flaw in the system

The Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in), a digital rights organization, said the growing reliance on automated takedowns raised serious concerns about transparency, accountability and due process.

"There is little transparency about the processes through which content is identified, flagged and restricted, or whether there is any meaningful human oversight before a takedown is implemented," SFLC.in told DW.

The organization also tested X's verification process by submitting a takedown request against one of its own posts using a fake email address. X registered the request, raising questions about how it verified the identity and authority of those submitting requests.
After SFLC.in alerted the company, X introduced email verification codes for people submitting takedown requests.
"A channel that lets anyone pose as a law enforcement official can be misused to silence lawful speech," SFLC.in said.
X did not respond to DW's request for a comment.
Government says no censorship
The Indian government denies that it is censoring online content.

While the ministry did not respond to DW's latest request for a comment, in an email response to DW in August, Vinod Kumar, chief of media and communications at the Information Technology Ministry, said Instagram posts by students and protesters following the July CJP protests "are not being taken down as alleged."
"Media enjoys freedom in India. The Government does not censor online content," Kumar said, adding that the government only acts against "objectionable content."
Under the Indian IT rules, "unlawful content" generally refers to material which could threaten India's sovereignty and integrity, disturb public order, incite violence, or constitute defamation.

However, social media influencers such as university professor Madri Kakoti, alias Dr. Medusa, continue to report restrictions. Kakoti's Instagram account was restricted in India on November 16 without notice, she said, along with that of satirist Shamita Yadav.

blocks.caption: Screenshot of the Instagram account 'the.ranting.gola' showing that the account is not available in IndiaImage: Screenshot Instagram/the.ranting.gola

blocks.text: The price of free speech
Rights groups including Human Rights Watch have warned that expanding content restrictions could chill free expression and encourage self-censorship among journalists, creators and ordinary users.
Acharya, however, said he would continue his work.
"The Indian Constitution gives me the right to draw political cartoons," he said. "It's totally democratic to question and criticize the government in India."

For Tiwari, the issue goes beyond the reach of a single video. It is also about preserving a record of what happened, after the Delhi Police denied allegations of using excessive force during the July 20 protest in front of the Supreme Court.
"We have seen several other videos now, and it's well established why that girl was crying, and that the Delhi Police used force and lied about it," she said.

"Still, I want that video back up because it needs to stay for posterity. I think that's the larger idea: they want to take this stuff down so it fades from memory, allowing them to categorically deny it later when we have little left to show for what happened."
India's 'Cockroach' protesters claim online censorship

articles.title: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What to know
articles.summary: The ICJ is set to decide whether Myanmar's military operations in Rakhine State a decade ago were carried out with the intent to destroy the country's Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

image.caption: Proving Myanmar's intent behind the alleged atrocities is the key question the ICJ is grappling withImage: Mouneb Taim/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver on Thursday its long-awaited judgment in The Gambia's landmark genocide case against Myanmar, seven years after the case was lodged in The Hague.
The Gambia filed the case with the United Nations' top court in November 2019, formally accusing the Southeast Asian nation of breaking its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

In documents and hearings, The Gambia has alleged that Myanmar waged a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder in Rakhine State from 2016 to 2017, intending to wipe out the area's ethnic Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

A UN fact-finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. Another 700,000 Rohingya fled the country to neighboring Bangladesh, where most of them still live today in the world's largest refugee settlement.

Even before 2016, the predominantly Muslim Rohingya had been subjected to decades of persecution by the Buddhist-majority country's government, with many forced into resettlement camps and most denied citizenship.
A number of cases over Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya have been filed in courts around the world. The ICJ will be the first to issue a ruling.

"The Rohingya people have been waiting for justice for decades for the atrocities and crimes committed against [us]. There were no venues available in [Myanmar]…. International venues were the only hope," said Aung Kyaw Moe, a prominent Rohingya activist whose family was forced to flee the country during the pogroms.
"We've come over many years to a situation where a judgment will be delivered, and the expectation from the Rohingya community is very high," he said.
Rohingya caught in the middle of Myanmar's civil war
Journey to judgment day

A month after The Gambia lodged its case with the ICJ in 2019, Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar's de facto civilian leader at the time, traveled to The Hague to contest the allegations, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
The move tarnished her international reputation as a human rights icon. Many human rights advocates criticized her for defending the very military that had persecuted her for most of her life.

In 2020, ahead of a final judgment, the ICJ issued emergency "provisional measures" ordering Myanmar to take all steps "within its power" to prevent acts of genocide against the Rohingya, an order rights groups say it has blatantly ignored.
Myanmar's military went on to oust the country's democratically elected government the following year, placing Aung San Suu Kyi under arrest and setting off a bloody civil war that continues to rage.
Myanmar also challenged both the court's jurisdiction over the alleged crimes and The Gambia's right to lodge the case, both of which the ICJ rejected in 2022.

The ICJ then held 14 days of hearings this January for Myanmar and The Gambia to make their arguments before the panel. While Myanmar called one witness, The Gambia called three, as well as an expert.
A question of intent

As The Gambia has accused Myanmar of breaking several articles of the Genocide Convention, Thursday's judgment could be "fairly complicated," said Melanie O'Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia and past president of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

The convention outlines that states have a duty to prevent and punish genocide and to establish effective penalties for those found responsible. The ICJ could rule in Myanmar's favor on some of these provisions and against it on others.

"So, there's quite a lot of layers here. They'll be looking at all of those issues, along with, of course, delving into the facts of the case and the individual crimes of genocide and whether or not Myanmar committed those individual crimes with the intent to destroy the Rohingya," O'Brien said.
Bangladesh: Could the UN help the Rohingya return home?
Proving Myanmar's intent behind the alleged atrocities is the key question the ICJ is grappling with.
Myanmar argues that its actions were strictly part of a legitimate counterinsurgency and counterterrorism operation, and that those actions could not at the same time be judged as acts of genocide.

Days before the Myanmar military launched its heaviest operations in Rakhine, in August 2017, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group based in the state, staged a coordinated attack on more than 30 police posts, killing several officers.
Either-or, maybe both

The Gambia argues that Myanmar's actions can qualify as both counterinsurgency and genocide at the same time. It also argues that the sexual violence and killing of children that accompanied the operations are proof that genocide was part of the goal.

"It directly undermines Myanmar's argument that this was a legitimate counterterrorism operation," said Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin and a former associate legal officer at the ICJ.

"Because evidence of those types of atrocities are very hard to square with the idea that this had some other purpose beyond terrorizing the Rohingya population and indeed taking actions to try to destroy them," he said.
O'Brien and Becker said The Gambia's case against Myanmar is a chance for the ICJ to clarify how it weighs such circumstantial or indirect evidence when judging whether genocide has taken place.
Because investigators were denied access to Rakhine State, they had to rely on interviews with victims and witnesses who had fled Myanmar and on reports by the UN and other groups.

"And how the court deals with that, whether the ICJ accepts or rejects The Gambia's view or Myanmar's view of genocidal intent and how you prove it, this will have major repercussions for other cases," said Becker.
Rohingya women in Bangladeshi camps lack toilets
Justice denied vs. delayed
The ICJ is grappling with some of the same questions in cases between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, Ukraine and Russia, and South Africa and Israel.
"I'm sure that the parties in the other cases will pick up on what the court rules in this case and add it to their own cases," said O'Brien.
"And even though this case will only be binding on The Gambia and Myanmar, the court itself may also refer to its own law in their future cases," she added.
The ICJ's judgment may have some effect on not only other cases but other courts as well.

The International Criminal Court — which, unlike the ICJ, tries individuals and not states — is considering an arrest warrant request for Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in a trial on alleged crimes against humanity committed against the Rohingya. Becker and O'Brien say a finding of genocide by the ICJ could bolster the case for granting the warrant.
What a finding of genocide would actually do for the Rohingya is another key question.

Enforcing any reparations or restitution the court may order would rest with the UN Security Council. But with China and Russia, both allies of Min Aung Hlaing's regime, holding veto power on the council, there are serious doubts about whether it would act on any court order on Myanmar.
Aung Kyaw Moe remains hopeful that the Rohingya will one day receive justice.

"Despite these challenges, there are a lot of hopes that we can [move] toward the betterment of the Rohingya people, including compensation, reparations, transitional justice in the domestic setting in the long term," he said.

articles.title: Boy, three, dies after ‘medical emergency’ at Greater Manchester nursery
articles.summary:
Police are investigating death of child three days after emergency services were called to Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton

A three-year-old boy has died after a “medical emergency” at a…
articles.byline: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent

blocks.text: A three-year-old boy has died after a “medical emergency” at a nursery in Greater Manchester.
Emergency services were called to Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton, near Manchester on the afternoon of 2 November after “reports of a concern for a child”.

Greater Manchester police said at the time that a child had been taken to hospital after a “medical emergency” and was in a critical condition. An air ambulance landed close to the building, while three police vehicles, an ambulance and a rapid response paramedic car were also dispatched.

Police confirmed on Wednesday that the child, who has not been named, died three days later. “Sadly, the boy passed away on Thursday 5 November,” GMP said in a statement. “His family is being supported by specialist officers during this incredibly difficult time.”

An investigation had been opened, GMP said, adding that “no arrests have made in that time”. The force said the investigation was in line with usual procedure, “as the circumstances leading up to the boy’s death occurred in a care setting”.
Det Ch Insp Claire Brennan said: “This is an incredibly tragic development in a deeply upsetting incident and our thoughts remain with the boy’s family.

“We are in the very early stages of our involvement and are carefully considering events and the evidence available to us. For now, we ask that the family’s privacy is respected as they begin to navigate the unimaginable loss of their little boy.”

Cosy Toes runs four nurseries in Middleton, providing childcare for children up to five years old. GMP has asked anyone with information that could help the investigation to make a report online, or call 0161 856 3635.
Details can also be given anonymously to the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or by filling out a form on their website.

Cosy Toes has been approached for comment.

articles.title: UK government ‘breaking the law’ by not stopping decline of wild birds
articles.summary:
Populations at lowest level on record with 45% of native breeding species in decline, environment regulator says

Environment secretary Angela Eagle, her ministers and Natural England are…

blocks.text: Environment secretary Angela Eagle, her ministers and Natural England are breaking the law by failing to intervene to slow the catastrophic decline of Britain’s wild birds, the UK’s environment regulator has said.
New data shows wild bird populations have dropped to their lowest level on record, with almost half – 45% – of 132 native breeding species in decline over a five-year period.
In the last five decades, Britain has lost more than 73 million wild birds from its landscape, according to the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO).
The loss of wild birds includes some of Britain’s best-loved garden birds, including swifts, turtledoves and tree sparrows, as well as wood warblers and bullfinches.

Ministers have legal responsibilities to take action to recover bird populations to healthy levels, as well as specific duties to designate Special Protection Areas (SPAs) where birds and their habitats are legally protected.

But the Office for Environmental Protection (OEP), the independent environmental regulator, said on Wednesday that the environment secretary, her department and Natural England were all breaking the law by failing to protect wild birds.
Eagle has breached environmental law by failing to classify new SPAs, extend existing sites or add new species to those that are protected, the regulator said.

Natural England is in breach of environmental law, according to the OEP, by failing to take the action needed to maintain or restore wild bird populations to appropriate levels and ensure they have sufficient habitats.
The government’s independent nature adviser is also accused of breaching the law by failing to carry out a review of whether there is sufficient habitat for wild birds.

The OEP said the review was important because it was supposed to provide an expert and independent assessment of whether there is sufficient diversity and area of habitat for wild birds, as well as to identify gaps and explain what action is needed to support their recovery.

The continued decline in bird populations comes despite evidence that the public’s interest and attention to wild birds is growing. In May, the RSPB reported a 47% increase in the number of people enjoying bird watching over the past eight years.
Helen Venn, chief regulatory officer for the OEP, said there have been continued delays by ministers to protect bird populations.

“As a nation of bird-lovers, and with birds acting as important indicators for the state of our nature more widely, the latest statistics showing declines in the populations of some of our most treasured species are deeply concerning,” said Venn.

“This is why it is important that Defra and Natural England do carry out their legal responsibilities in a reasonable timeframe to deliver nature recovery and in relation to the classification and adaptation of SPAs on land.
after newsletter promotion

“Continued delay has left a significant number of sites for wild bird populations without the levels of protection they need and allowed the scale of the actions needed to deliver a sufficient SPA network to build up.”
There are 82 SPAs in England, as well as six cross-border and offshore sites.
The government is legally bound to expand and increase protected areas across the country as part of its 30 by 30 commitment to protect at least 30% of land and seas for nature’s recovery by 2030.

But despite repeated promises by Labour’s environment ministers, wild bird populations across the UK are showing no sign of widespread recovery, with both short and long-term trends indicating that nearly half of all species are in decline, according to Defra’s latest statistics.

Beccy Speight, the RSPB’s chief executive, said: “We now expect urgent action, including the designation of new and extended Special Protection Areas and other targeted measures for species such as curlew, bittern and hen harrier, which are in most need. Successive governments right across the UK have known about these problems for years. The time for navel gazing has long passed; the time for taking action is now, before it is too late.”
The Department for Environment was approached for comment.

articles.title: Business Council of Australia more aligned with fossil fuel industry than its members’ values, analysis finds
articles.summary:
Research by InfluenceMap raises questions about association’s policies and representation, particularly around advocacy for new gas supplies

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Business Council of Australia is lobbying for gas expansion policies that clash with the climate concerns of the majority of its own members, according to new research that raises questions about the sway of a handful of major companies.

The business association also does not publicly disclose who is on its energy and climate committee, prompting transparency concerns among researchers over how its policies are shaped and whose interests they represent.

Analysis by London-headquartered InfluenceMap found the BCA’s positions aligned more closely with energy companies Woodside, Santos and ConocoPhillips than with the majority of its corporate base, particularly on the energy transition where it has advocated for new gas supplies over phasing down.
InfluenceMap’s Australia lead, Jack Herring, said major associations such as the BCA are an influential voice in government policymaking.
“These findings suggest the BCA’s climate policy engagement better reflects the narrow interests of members connected to the fossil fuel value chain than its wider membership,” Herring said.

“Advocacy for fossil gas expansion risks undermining Australia’s climate targets and also threatens to create increased health risks and energy affordability and security concerns for everyday households, so this is an issue that affects us all.”

InfluenceMap’s analysis of company positions shows more than two-thirds of the members assessed, including Qantas, Woolworths, Coles, Atlassian, Fortescue and major banks CBA and NAB, advocate for stronger climate policies than the business council itself.
That support typically includes backing faster renewable energy rollout and advocating for more ambitious emission reduction targets.

For the study, the thinktank assessed 58 companies – a representative sample of the BCA’s more than 120 members – drawing on thousands of public statements, government submissions and regulatory filings.
Of those members assessed, 69% backed stronger climate policies than the BCA, a gap that widened to 78% on energy transition issues.
Herring said the BCA does not disclose who sits on its internal climate and energy committees, obscuring how its policy positions are formed.
“We obviously do know who’s on the association board, but beyond that, there’s no transparency around those internal committees,” he said.

A spokesperson for the BCA said the association supported the “national goal of achieving net zero by 2050 and the setting of interim targets, while also delivering reliable and affordable energy and ensuring we don’t undermine our international competitiveness along the way”.
“The BCA has long advocated for gas as an essential part of the net zero transition – ensuring grid stability – while we move to greater reliance on renewable energy,” the spokesperson said.
The BCA declined to comment on the makeup of its climate and energy committee.
after newsletter promotion
‘Technology agnostic’

The analysis comes as industry groups ramp up lobbying over the “safeguard mechanism”, Australia’s main policy for curbing emissions from its largest industrial facilities, which is under federal review.

While the BCA and most big resources companies publicly support the Paris agreement and Australia’s net zero 2050 carbon emissions target, they interpret what those commitments require in radically different ways to what is widely regarded as climate best practice.

Several oil and gas producer members, including Woodside, argue that increased gas supply is required to support the shift to renewables and enhance energy security in language that has been adopted by the BCA.

This rubs against those BCA members aligned with the findings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which found greenhouse gas emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure were more than enough to push the world beyond its climate goals.

InfluenceMap also found that the business council frequently lobbies for a “technology-neutral” or “technology agnostic” energy transition, which is the same language used by the fossil fuel sector designed to steer renewable energy funding toward gas.

Persephone Fraser, the ethical research and climate policy lead at fund manager Australian Ethical, said misaligned lobbying was a significant risk for companies and their shareholders, and a major risk to the economy.
“Companies must be scrutinising what is being advocated for in their name and actively correcting the record when it is inconsistent with their own positions, and interests,” Fraser said.
“Membership of an industry association cannot mean outsourcing responsibility for climate lobbying.”
Do you know more? Contact jonathan.barrett@theguardian.com

articles.title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
articles.summary: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.

blocks.text: Image source, David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each.
If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
Dario Amodei

blocks.caption: Dario Amodei wears a grey suit and patterned tie flanked by bodyguards.

blocks.text: Image source, Finn Gomez/Getty Images
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

items: Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profile

blocks.text: Daniela Amodei

blocks.caption: Daniela Amodei wears a jacket and sits in an offfice

blocks.text: Image source, Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown

blocks.caption: Tom Brown stands on a stage in front of a US flag wearing a dark suit and tie.

blocks.text: Image source, Cornell Watson/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark

blocks.caption: Jack Clark stands on a stage wearing a suit and shirt

blocks.text: Image source, Peerapon Boonyakiat/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Jared Kaplan

blocks.caption: Jared Kaplan wears a biege teeshirt and sits on a stage talking into a small headset microphone

blocks.text: Image source, Chris J. Ratcliffe/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Chris Olah

blocks.caption: Chris Olah wears a dark suit and striped tie, and speaks into a microphone sitting in a comfy chair.

blocks.text: Image source, Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty Images
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left Toronto University early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.
Sam McCandlish

blocks.caption: Sam McCandlish wears a suit and tie

blocks.text: Image source, Anthropic

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

articles.title: Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions
articles.summary:
Israeli diplomats say decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by caretaker government led by Netanyahu

Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large…

blocks.text: Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.

Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.

She ordered the Israel land authority and ministry of housing not to open the tender process. Israeli diplomats suggested the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had acted prematurely on Monday in sanctioning the eight construction firms. But UK diplomats believe the growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.

The deferral puts the E1 settlement expansion in the mix for any coalition negotiations. The leader of the Change bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has been clear in opposing violent settler activity, as has the newly elected Knesset speaker, Matan Kahana, an ally of Eisenkot.

Eisenkot has also opposed the E1 settlement expansion, describing it as a mistake likely to alienate international opinion. He said of the plan: “I recall that Netanyahu himself opposed this for a long time, and due to coalition pressure, he gave in and approved it.”

blocks.caption: Palestinian Bedouin boys play football in Jabal al-Baba, near Ma’aleh Adumim, in the area marked for the E1 settlement. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: The EI settlement expansion, due to have been announced on Thursday, has long been seen as qualitatively different since the land – between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents – bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem.

Miliband has said it would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state. The UK, along with a group of European countries, has recently recognised Palestine, and the preservation of a two-state solution has been described as the north star of Labour policy towards the region.

The construction tender was published for more than 3,401 housing units in the area. At the beginning of November, the Israel Defense Forces began demolishing homes in a Bedouin community within the E1 area.

blocks.caption: A Palestinian Bedouin walks up a hill in Jabal al-Baba, where development of the planned E1 settlement will displace several Bedouin communities. Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: Israel has already enforced the downgrading of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem as a reprisal for Miliband’s decision in September to try to end trade links with the illegal settlements.
after newsletter promotion

Bennett said: “The British Labour government’s hostility, bias and one-sided approach are particularly glaring given its failure to take any action against the Palestinian Authority, which continues to encourage terrorism through financial payments, promote incitement in its education system and engage in illegal construction in violation of signed agreements.”

Although the Israeli election was largely fought on domestic security-related issues, Eisenkot seems to be more sensitive to the implications of Israel’s crumbling global reputation, and the need to make efforts to be seen to be listening to the criticism. If he becomes prime minister, Eisenkot will, indirectly at least, also have to take account of the views of the Arab parties even if these parties are not going to become members of the government.

The group Peace Now welcomed the attorney general’s decision: “A government that lost the elections is not permitted to exploit its final days in power to advance destructive moves that will endanger Israel’s future and its international standing. Construction in E1 is liable to eliminate the possibility of a two-state solution and drag Israel into a severe diplomatic crisis and international sanctions. The AG’s decision is an important step, but the struggle is not over yet.”

articles.title: Ministers to drop foie gras imports ban to help seal EU food trade deal
articles.summary:
Animal welfare charities criticise ‘backwards step’ on foie gras, production of which has been banned in UK since 2007

Ministers will drop plans to ban foie gras imports into the UK in order…

blocks.text: Ministers will drop plans to ban foie gras imports into the UK in order to smooth a trade deal with the EU that will be announced this week.

As first reported by the Financial Times, the proposed ban will be officially dropped on Friday when the government announces its sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) trade deal with the EU to reduce checks and paperwork on imports and exports of food and drink with the bloc.

Labour promised before coming to power that it would ban foie gras imports. Before the election, Steve Reed, the then shadow environment secretary, said Labour would “ban the commercial import of foie gras, where ducks and geese are aggressively force-fed”. He labelled the practice “beyond disgusting”.

Foie gras is made by force-feeding ducks and geese grain through a funnel or tube that has been thrust down the bird’s neck – a process known as gavage that swells the animal’s liver to many times its normal size. The livers are then harvested.

Banning it has proved difficult as EU countries including France produce and export the product and are against other members putting in place an import ban. The Guardian reported earlier this year that ministers were preparing to drop the ban in order to secure concessions.

Sustainability chefs and animal welfare charities have criticised the U-turn. Boris Johnson’s government promised to use the powers granted by Brexit to ban the “cruel” product, which still appears on menus across the country almost seven years after the UK officially left the EU.

Some restaurants still sell foie gras but many shops have removed it from sale, including the king’s grocer, Fortnum & Mason, which took it off shelves in 2021. The production of foie gras has been banned in the UK since 2007.

The French chef Alexis Gauthier used to sell more foie gras than any other restaurant in London before converting to a vegan diet and menu. He now sells a mushroom-based “faux gras” to customers of his Soho restaurant, who include the former Beatle Paul McCartney. Gauthier said the ban being dropped was “terrible news”.
“I find it very sad our government capitulates so easily,” he said. “The cruelty of foie gras belongs firmly in the history books, not in a progressive society in 2026.”

Will Murray, a co-founder of the sustainable British restaurant Fallow, also based in London, serves a mushroom parfait rather than foie gras. He said: “This feels like a step in the wrong direction with regards to animal welfare. I think London diners aren’t really asking for a big return of foie gras on menus.”

David Bowles, the head of public affairs at the RSPCA, said: “We are extremely disappointed that farm animal welfare laws have been put on the chopping block as part of this new deal. Any suggestions plans to act on foie gras are being shelved to ease EU realignment are deeply concerning for animals and would be a clear backwards step.”

A spokesperson for the charity Four Paws said: “The UK prohibited the production of foie gras nearly 20 years ago because of the serious animal welfare concerns associated with force-feeding ducks and geese. Yet foie gras produced using these same methods can still be imported and sold here. As the UK strengthens its relationship with the EU, animal welfare must not become a casualty of closer trade ties.”

Government insiders indicated that the ban would be dropped but noted that the method of production was banned in the UK. A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said the method raises welfare concerns.

They said: “We are negotiating a food and drink deal that will slash red tape and costly paperwork, make it easier and cheaper to export seafood, boost the British economy by up to £5bn a year, and back British businesses and jobs. We are working closely with businesses to ensure a smooth transition so they can make the most of the benefits this deal unlocks.”

articles.title: Man arrested in Nashville after DNA links him to unsolved 1990s rape cases
articles.summary:
Archibald Amory, 58, reportedly being held in Tennessee pending return to New York, where he was tied to two cases

A man has been arrested in

blocks.text: A man has been arrested in Nashville after DNA linked him to a series of unsolved New York City rapes from the 1990s, according to a news report.

Archibald Amory, 58, was detained on Thursday in Hermitage, a neighborhood of Nashville, and is being held there pending his return to New York City, according to the Daily News, citing sources and Nashville authorities.

Amory has been linked via DNA to two rapes that took place in Queens, and connected to several other uncharged sex assaults. Sources said recent advances in DNA technology and investigative methods helped identify Amory.

Court papers filed in Tennessee said special victims investigators in Nashville and with the NYPD “identified Archibald Amory as a wanted fugitive in connection to a series of rape investigations originating in the jurisdiction of New York City”.
Armory appeared in court in Nashville on Monday, according to a spokesperson for the district attorney of Davidson county. He is currently being held on $800,000 bond.
Another man has also been arrested, in Miami, for allegedly raping a woman in New York’s Central Park last month.
Dereck Rivera-Deleon, 30, was arrested on Tuesday at a Miami Burger King where he had been working. Police said he will also be charged in two other Central Park rapes.
Rivera-Deleon will be charged with the sexual assault of a 39-year-old woman who was walking just outside Central Park on 24 October when he pulled a knife on her near E 66th Street and Fifth Avenue.

The suspect allegedly dragged the victim into the park, where he raped her, before a bystander, who witnessed the attack, called 911. Rivera-Deleon was identified as the attacker via surveillance film, and investigators have linked him to a Central Park rape in 2023 and another in 2021.

articles.title: Kuwait says it repelled first Iranian attack in two months after US strikes island
articles.summary: Bahrain says it was also attacked by Iran following a US air strike on the Iranian island of Qeshm in the Gulf on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise.

The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage.
It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday.
The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war.
The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass.
On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage.

The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law".

"The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency.
Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks".
The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull.

Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions".
The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait.
Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran.
"If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said.

On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said.
Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure.

In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished.
Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route".

At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.

articles.title: Republicans could expedite bill to make big oil immune to lawsuits, warn experts
articles.summary:
GOP lawmakers are rushing through high-priority bills before newly elected Democrats are sworn in

Climate groups fear lawmakers could pass a bill by the end of the year that would give…

blocks.text: Climate groups fear lawmakers could pass a bill by the end of the year that would give fossil fuel companies immunity from lawsuits and legislation that aims to hold them accountable for the climate crisis.

After the blue wave election, Republican lawmakers are rushing to pass high-priority bills before newly elected Democrats are sworn in. Hundreds of elected leaders and climate groups sent a letter to Democratic leadership urging them to reject any proposal that would shield fossil fuel companies from liability for the climate crisis.

Iyla Shornstein, political director for the Center for Climate Integrity, said the election results showed voters don’t want this type of legislation. “Voters at the polls sent a clear message about how costs are impacting their everyday lives. Gas prices are skyrocketing, but why would we spend our time giving special treatment to big oil, who are also simultaneously enjoying record profits at our expense? … The elections sent a pretty clear message that our elected leaders need to be spending their time helping working families, not major corporations like big oil.”

In April, Republicans introduced the Stop Climate Shakedowns bill that would shield fossil fuel companies from various attempts to hold them accountable. Ted Cruz and Harriet Hageman, two Republican lawmakers, introduced companion Senate and House bills. “Radical environmental groups have waged a coordinated campaign to weaponize our judicial system against American energy producers, including many in Texas,” Cruz said in a statement announcing the Senate bill. “They’re using meritless lawsuits to bankrupt our energy industry, kill good paying jobs and drive up the cost of electricity and gasoline for hardworking families.”

Eleven states, two tribal governments and dozens of municipalities have filed lawsuits against big oil companies to hold them accountable for the climate emergency. The lawsuits are grounded in science that connects climate disasters to emissions from fossil fuel companies and increasing evidence that the companies deceived the public about their own internal science warning them about the dangers of fossil fuels.

Another accountability effort has come from states such as New York and Vermont that have passed climate superfund laws to recover costs by shifting the financial burden from climate disasters onto the fossil fuel companies that caused them. Both New York and Vermont’s superfund laws have faced opposition including challenges by the Department of Justice; a judge struck down the New York superfund law in September, the state’s governor, Kathy Hochul, is appealing.

The fossil fuel immunity bill has four key parts, said Shornstein: it would dismiss existing climate liability lawsuits against fossil fuel companies, prohibit new lawsuits, void climate superfund laws and assert that the federal government is the sole authority over the regulation of greenhouse gas emissions and climate crisis, which pre-empts states from acting on it.

Stopping climate lawsuits and superfund laws was a top priority for the American Petroleum Institute this year, but the bill stalled in September when the House judiciary committee failed to advance it.

Shornstein said Republican lawmakers could still rush through the bill or attach immunity language to other legislation before the end of the current Congress. “We’re at a critical moment, because Trump and the GOP and big oil’s allies want to bail out the fossil fuel industry while they still have power,” she said. “Immunity for big oil has been high on the list of priorities, so this is their last ditch effort.”

“We need to be extremely on our toes and vigilant and ready to mobilize to make sure that Congress rejects this sweeping giveaway to big oil,” said Kathy Mulvey, program director for fossil fuel accountability at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “I expect that they would see the lame duck session as a real opportunity to push through the Cruz-Hageman bill.”

The bill would block source attribution science, a growing field of science that connects climate disasters to the emissions of specific oil and gas companies. The bill says such scientific efforts “lack scientific credibility and are, therefore, arbitrary”.

“The fact that [they] are specifically going after this field of science and the scientists who are playing a leading role indicates really how much they’re threatened by being held accountable for the harms that they’re causing,” Mulvey said.

The immunity bill follows a pattern of powerful industries asking Congress to shield them from liability – although not all have succeeded. In the 1990s, when tobacco companies faced dozens of lawsuits seeking to recover costs from smoking-related illnesses, they unsuccessfully lobbied Congress to introduce legislation to shield them. And in 2005, in response to a wave of lawsuits attempting to hold gunmakers liable for violence, the National Rifle Association (NRA) achieved a lobbying victory when Congress passed a liability shield law, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act.

That gun law may have inspired the push for a big oil immunity law. In a letter last yeat to Pam Bondi, the former US attorney general, Republican state attorneys general asked for a liability shield for big oil, which they directly compared with the shield law for gun manufacturers. “The fossil fuel industry explicitly invokes the liability waiver given to the gun industry in 2005 as its model for what it’s trying to achieve,” said Mulvey.

At the state level, fossil fuel company allies are engaged in a similar effort to shield them from liability. A ProPublica investigation reported that immunity bills introduced in a number of Republican-controlled state houses were part of a coordinated effort by a rightwing network that included activist Leonard Leo and the American Legislative Exchange Council.

In a statement to ProPublica, Leo did not dispute the findings. “For decades, the left had leveraged immense resources to capture the institutions that shape our society,” he wrote in a text. “That takeover resulted in a radically woke culture that does not reflect the will of the American people, or the pillars of limited constitutional government that made our country great. That is why our enterprise supports organizations that are committed to crushing liberal dominance and restoring balance in the institutions that shape society.”

“We’re also seeing this push at the state level too,” Shornstein said. “There were five states that enacted legislation this cycle that provides pretty expansive legal protections to the industry. So they’re taking a very holistic, if you will, approach to escaping accountability.”
