articles.title: Waymo temporarily pulls robotaxis from U.S. highways
articles.summary: Waymo has temporarily stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways after California banned the vehicles from state freeways following recent traffic incidents.

image.caption: The Waymo Ojai autonomous vehicle, a Chinese-made electric vehicle manufactured by Zeekr, travels on Oct. 13 along a major Los Angeles freeway through Hawthorne, Calif., with a person sitting in the driver's seat. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New
Waymo has temporarily stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways after California banned the vehicles from state freeways following recent traffic incidents.
California called a halt after incidents at construction zones, Highway Patrol stops
The company had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, Ariz., and Austin, Texas.

A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an email that the company has "temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service," though it’s "continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel."
The suspension was implemented last Wednesday, according to the spokesperson, but they didn't say how long it would last.

The suspension came after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned the company’s robotaxis from freeways that same day. The ban followed two incidents including one in which three Waymo driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman said in a statement.
The construction zone incident occurred on Nov. 5 and the second, which involved California Highway Patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman.
Video of the Nov. 6 incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California Highway Patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break.
Most Torontonians wouldn't ride in a Waymo, new poll suggests

"The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," Groveman said.
Groveman added that "similar incidents" previously occurred on May 18.
The Waymo spokesperson said the "recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California" did not "involve any injuries or collisions."

California’s restrictions bar Waymo from operating and testing its driverless vehicles on California freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until "Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions."

items: Waymo is coming to Toronto. Will its self-driving cars be winter-ready?
Waymo’s driverless cars involved in 68% fewer crashes than human drivers, U.S. study finds

blocks.text: Waymo, the California-based company which is a subsidiary of Alphabet, offers rides on city streets in many other areas including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver, with plans to expand to American cities with more adverse winter conditions. There are also plans for international expansion, in cities that include Toronto.
In all cases, Waymo plans to begin fully autonomous commercial passenger service would require regulatory approval from the relevant governments where it seeks to operate.
A number of different companies around the world are involved in supplying parts and technology in Waymo's supply chain and production, including Magna International of Vaughan, Ont.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Jury was never told that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was barred from practising over concerns for patients’ safety

A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was…

blocks.text: A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial over fears he posed a risk to their safety.

Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that Letby had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told.

Among the reasons for UCLH’s decision was that his advice to child patients relating to insulin was not considered safe. A UCLH medical director told the General Medical Council, the doctors’ regulator, that the hospital could not “accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people”.

The GMC, which was already investigating Hindmarsh’s fitness to practise, subsequently applied for his registration as a doctor to be suspended. That could have resulted in his evidence in the trial of Letby – which was still in progress – being dismissed.

However, in April 2023 a medical practitioners tribunal – an independent panel that decides GMC proceedings against doctors – opted not to suspend his registration. Instead, it ordered that Hindmarsh be directly supervised in his work, to protect patient safety. That decision had no practical effect because UCLH had already barred him from practising at all.

While Hindmarsh’s ability to practise was being restricted, the trial of Letby continued at Manchester crown court. Her defence team was never informed that Hindmarsh’s hospital considered his professional judgment and practice so deficient as to be unsafe to child patients, or of the April 2023 tribunal ruling.

While Hindmarsh did inform Cheshire constabulary in December 2022 that he was subject to a GMC investigation, and in February 2023 the Crown Prosecution Service told Letby’s defence, her legal team was not made aware that he was later barred from practising on safety grounds.
Had they known, Letby’s defence team might have challenged his credibility as an expert witness and applied for the jury to be told or for his evidence to be dismissed.
Failures of disclosure are recognised as potential grounds for a CCRC referral and for convictions to be overturned.

The apparent lack of transparency could mean Hindmarsh breached legal rules requiring expert witnesses to disclose to the party instructing them any disciplinary proceedings against them and anything that may be considered to undermine their credibility. Hindmarsh declined to answer any of the Guardian’s questions about this, the hospitals’ concerns about him, or the GMC investigation.

blocks.caption: Lucy Letby has always maintained she is innocent. Photograph: Cheshire constabulary/AP

blocks.text: Letby, who was a neonatal nurse at the Countess of Chester hospital, was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, and sentenced to 15 whole-life terms in prison. Court of appeal judges turned down her applications to appeal.

She has always maintained she is innocent, and her lawyer Mark McDonald has applied to the Criminal Cases Review Commission, the miscarriages of justice watchdog, to send her case back to the court of appeal.

Since the convictions, dozens of leading UK and international medical experts have argued that the prosecution’s case, including Hindmarsh’s evidence, was wrong, and produced reports submitted in support of her CCRC application.

Dr Shoo Lee, a renowned Canadian neonatologist who argues that the prosecution misrepresented his research, last year made public the summary findings of a 14-member expert panel he had convened. They found unanimously that the babies died or collapsed due to natural causes and poor medical care on the unit, and that there was no evidence of murders, insulin poisoning or any other deliberate harm.

Seven experts have contributed to reports submitted by McDonald to the CCRC, contesting Hindmarsh’s opinions. They argue that Hindmarsh’s calculations and diagnoses of the babies’ medical conditions were factuallyinaccurate in many respects, and his opinion that insulin was infused via the fluid bags is not supported by the evidence. The experts also argue that blood tests known as immunoassays, relied on by the prosecution as definitive evidence of poisoning, are known to be fallible.

Lady Justice Thirlwall, who chaired a two-year public inquiry after the convictions, refused to consider the experts’ arguments that Letby may have suffered a miscarriage of justice, or to wait for the CCRC decision. She produced a report in September making a series of recommendations for the NHS, on the basis that Letby was guilty.
The insulin expert

Hindmarsh was presented to the Letby jury throughout as a distinguished authority. The lead barrister for the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), Nick Johnson KC, described him to jurors as “the pre-eminent expert” on insulin.
Hindmarsh was a consultant paediatric endocrinologist – a specialist in hormones, including insulin, in children – at UCLH from 1991, and a professor at UCL, with an eminent reputation.

When Johnson introduced Hindmarsh at the trial, he asked if he was also an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street. The jury was not told that four months earlier, in July 2022, Hindmarsh’s contract in that role at the children’s hospital had been terminated.

blocks.caption: Hindmarsh’s contract at Great Ormond Street hospital was terminated in July 2022. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Hindmarsh asserted in his trial evidence that blood tests and the medical records of two babies being cared for at the Countess of Chester hospital showed they had been poisoned with insulin, most likely inserted into intravenous fluid bags. The prosecution alleged that Letby injected insulin into the bags, although there was no direct or forensic evidence that she or anybody else had done so.

Hindmarsh’s evidence alleging insulin poisoning was considered pivotal to the convictions. In summing up, the judge, James Goss, told the jury that if they were sure babies were being deliberately harmed, they could decide other babies were also being harmed, even if they were not sure about the precise cause.

Johnson presented the two cases of alleged insulin poisoning as incontrovertible evidence. The charges of attempted murder of those two babies were the first on which the jury reached guilty verdicts, and two of only three unanimous guilty verdicts.
‘Multiple and wide-ranging concerns’
The Guardian first revealed in March that the GMC launched an investigation into Hindmarsh on 25 November 2022, the same day he first gave evidence as an expert for the prosecution of Letby.

Great Ormond Street hospital had reported “multiple and wide-ranging concerns” to the GMC, including Hindmarsh’s “diagnosis and treatment of patients” and “cases where harm to patients has been alleged”. UCLH had been leading a formal investigation of its own into Hindmarsh, and in December 2022 it reported its similar concerns to the GMC.

blocks.caption: University College Hospital in London. The trust reported its concerns to the GMC in December 2022. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA

blocks.text: Then in January 2023, while the Letby trial was still ongoing, a medical tribunal imposed orders that while the GMC investigation continued, Hindmarsh could only work at UCLH, and his clinical work had to be supervised, because otherwise he “may pose a real risk to members of the public”.

Until now, it has not been publicly known that UCLH reported further serious concerns on 15 March 2023, and informed the GMC it had excluded Hindmarsh from treating patients at all. This was less than three weeks after Hindmarsh had given his second and final day of evidence at Letby’s trial, on 24 February.

Documents seen by the Guardian show that a UCLH medical director, Dr Tim Hodgson, informed the GMC of the hospital’s decision. Hodgson wrote that Hindmarsh had breached the supervision order and given independent medical advice relating to three child patients, two involving insulin and diabetes. Hindmarsh’s medical colleagues had submitted “written concerns” about him, Hodgson said.

“On the grounds of safety UCLH are not presently in a position to allow Professor [Hindmarsh] to practice clinically even under supervision,” he wrote. “… I do not believe UCLH can accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people even with close clinical supervision.”

In two of the cases, Hodgson said Hindmarsh had independently advised the families that the children stop being given insulin at home. One of the children had an episode of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a critical, life-threatening complication caused by a severe lack of insulin.
“The patient had an episode of DKA and it’s not clear whether this coincided with the alleged advice from Professor Hindmarsh,” Hodgson wrote.

In the two insulin cases, Hodgson highlighted concerns that Hindmarsh was over-focusing on rare causes of hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) and diabetes (a cause of high blood sugar). In the first case, his colleagues believed Hindmarsh was not addressing more common causes of diabetes, and in the second, that he was “not treating high glucose levels appropriately”.
Had Letby’s defence team been informed of this, it could have strengthened the case for an application to inform the jury or exclude Hindmarsh’s evidence.

Experts who have provided reports for Letby’s CCRC application have argued that Hindmarsh’s opinion that the babies were poisoned via their fluid bags was an extremely unlikely explanation for their condition. They argue that Hindmarsh failed to recognise more common, identifiable medical causes.
Hodgson also said Hindmarsh had questioned the reliability of an insulin blood test result, sharing “his concern with the family that this was an erroneous, fallible test”.

This too could have been significant to Letby’s defence. At the trial, Johnson presented results from the immunoassay blood tests as definitive and said there was “no doubt” the two babies were poisoned.
after newsletter promotion

Experts supporting Letby’s CCRC application say immunoassays are known to be fallible because they can react to antibodies in blood to give a falsely high insulin result. Hodgson’s report suggests Hindmarsh recognised that blood tests for insulin were fallible, but he never made this clear at Letby’s trial.
The duty to disclose

The GMC responded to these new concerns by applying to the tribunal for Hindmarsh’s registration as a doctor to be suspended. Hindmarsh’s barrister argued stronglythat although he would not be treating patients because UCLH had excluded him, he should be allowed to continue working as an expert witness. Suspension, she said, would impede his ability to do so.
The barrister argued to the tribunal that Hindmarsh had not breached the supervision order and “no harm has been caused to patients”.

The three-person tribunal said it could not determine whether the previous supervision order had “technically” been breached. “However, the tribunal felt that the three cases identified by UCLH did raise concerns about patient safety,” it said.

blocks.caption: ‘I do not believe UCLH can accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose …,’ a medical director wrote. Photograph: Peter Summers/Getty Images

blocks.text: The tribunal decided that to suspend Hindmarsh would be disproportionate and explicitly allowed him to continue working as an expert witness, saying its order should not “restrict his non-clinical work”.

Instead, it imposed a tightening of the supervision requirement so that Hindmarsh from then had to be directly supervised when treating patients. This appears to have been a theoretical measure, however, because Hindmarsh was already restricted to only working for UCLH, and the hospital had barred him from treating patients at all.

Expert witnesses have a legal duty under the criminal procedure rules to tell the party instructing them – in Hindmarsh’s case, Cheshire constabulary – anything “that might reasonably be thought capable of undermining the expert’s opinion or detract from the credibility or impartiality of the expert”. This includes any disciplinary proceedings by a regulatory body.
The rules were introduced in 2014 to improve the reliability of expert evidence and guard against miscarriages of justice, after a series of wrongful convictions in the late 1990s and 2000s.
Lawyers have told the Guardian that under the rules, Hindmarsh should have told the police of the April 2023 tribunal ruling and that his hospital had barred him from clinical practice.

Tim Green KC, a specialist in disclosure, told the Guardian: “Whilst I cannot comment on the facts behind this complex and sensitive case, it is clear that the duty of an expert witness to make disclosure in a criminal or civil case of all material capable of undermining his opinion or detracting from his credibility is a continuous one.

“This duty extends after he has given evidence and through to the end of the proceedings. The duty continues through to any appeals, and arguably remains extant now, during the current considerations of the CCRC.

“Further restrictions imposed by a professional disciplinary tribunal on an expert’s right to practise, like those which can be imposed by the medical practitioners tribunal, are also disclosable in my view. Such restrictions are likely to be relevant to an assessment made by a jury or judge of an expert’s opinion evidence, competence and skill. For the same reasons, it also arguable that the information which led the tribunal to impose those restrictions in the first place is also disclosable.”

Lawyers have said Hindmarsh may have had a duty to tell the police and CPS initially, earlier in 2022, of the investigation into his practice led by UCLH, and that Great Ormond Street had terminated his contract. He does not appear to have done so.

blocks.caption: A court artist’s drawing of the prosecutor Nick Johnson KC cross-examining Lucy Letby during her retrial on a charge of attempted murder in June 2024. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA

blocks.text: When Johnson, the lead prosecutor, first introducedHindmarsh in court on 25 November 2022, he sought to clarify that the professor had an eminent position at Great Ormond Street as well as UCLH. After two questions not answered clearly, Johnson asked Hindmarsh: “Are you an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street hospital though?” Hindmarsh replied: “Yes. At that stage, yes.”
Hindmarsh did not say his contract at Great Ormond Street had been terminated four months earlier. That point was never clarified to the jury.
Hindmarsh was first informed of the GMC investigation into him on 30 November 2022. By this point, he had already made his first appearance in the Letby trial.

He told Cheshire constabulary two weeks later, on 14 December 2022. The CPS was informed two months later and told Letby’s then barrister, Ben Myers KC, on 20 February 2023, just four days before Hindmarsh was due to give his second day of evidence.

The CPS told Myers it would oppose the jury being told, because the GMC investigation into Hindmarsh had not reached a final adjudication. Myers did not then make an application to the judge for the jury to be informed.

On 23 February 2023, the day before Hindmarsh was due to return and give evidence, Johnson reminded the jury about him. “Professor Peter Hindmarsh will be here tomorrow to deal with the issue of insulin,” Johnson said. “And because he’s the pre-eminent expert in that narrow field, we will call him first.”

In July 2023, the judge referred to Hindmarsh’s evidence in his summing up. He did not mention Great Ormond Street at all, describing Hindmarsh as “emeritus professor of endocrinology at University College London and also a consultant paediatric endocrinologist at University College London hospitals”. Apparently unknown to the judge, UCLH had excluded Hindmarsh from practising as a consultant four months earlier.

Letby was convicted in August 2023. The GMC investigation into Hindmarsh never reached a final determination. In November 2024 Hindmarsh applied to remove himself from registration as a doctor. The GMC allowed this, a process known as “voluntary erasure”, which meant the investigation was stopped with no final adjudication.

The CPS has confirmed to the Guardian that it did not disclose to the defence anything relating to Hindmarsh being barred from clinical practice or the April 2023 tribunal ruling, because it had not been made aware of it.

Cheshire constabulary declined to provide information to the Guardian, so it is not clear whether Hindmarsh did or did not tell the police. Either way, it was not passed to the CPS, which would have disclosed it to Letby’s defence.
“Cheshire constabulary will not be commenting further in relation to this case,” a spokesperson said.
A CPS spokesperson said: “The CPS met all its disclosure obligations and no objections were raised by the defence at any stage in relation to expert evidence relied on by the prosecution.”

The CPS’ statement is made on the basis that it disclosed what it knew to the defence, and it had not been told about the tribunal ruling or that Hindmarsh was barred from treating patients. Johnson’s representatives did not reply to questions from the Guardian.

McDonald, Letby’s lawyer, said: “Peter Hindmarsh’s evidence was pivotal to the prosecution’s case against Lucy Letby. The insulin allegations were not simply another part of the prosecution’s case; they were its cornerstone, presented as scientific proof that she had deliberately poisoned babies and was capable of murder.

“It shaped the jury’s perception of Lucy and provided the lens through which they were invited to view every other allegation. This was not evidence that could be neatly confined to two convictions. Its influence permeated the entire trial. If the foundations of the insulin cases are unsafe, the consequences for the safety of the wider convictions cannot be overstated.”

The Guardian asked Hindmarsh detailed questions about the hospitals’ concerns, UCLH excluding him from clinical practice, and the GMC investigation, and put to him that he appeared not to have made adequate disclosure under the criminal procedure rules.
A representative for Hindmarsh replied: “He has no comment in relation to these questions and points.”

articles.title: Trump shakes hands with Putin and Xi ahead of historic talks in China
articles.summary: The three leaders will meet together for the first time on Thursday during a closely-watched summit.

blocks.text: Watch: BBC correspondents discuss historic Trump, Xi and Putin meeting
ByOlivia Ireland and Laura BickerChina correspondent
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin met for the first time in over a year on Wednesday, as the pair prepared for landmark talks in China with Xi Jinping.

The US president was greeted off his plane by the Chinese leader as he arrived in Shenzhen for a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders, which will culminate in a closely-watched meeting between the pair and the Russian president.
After a carefully choreographed handshake and hug between Trump and Xi on the tarmac, the US president later greeted and exchanged pleasantries with Putin ahead of a reception.
Trump and Putin are expected to hold one-on-one talks on the sidelines of the summit on Thursday, in which the conflict in Ukraine could be discussed.
However the main focus during the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (Apec) will be on the US-China-Russia talks on Thursday - the first time the trio of leaders have met together in person.

A full agenda has not been made public but there have been various hints about what could be discussed, including the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions and developments in artificial intelligence.

blocks.caption: Image caption, After a lavish reception from Xi, the leaders of the US and Russia shook hands ahead of a reception

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
After a lavish reception from Xi, the leaders of the US and Russia shook hands ahead of a reception
It was not clear on Wednesday what form separate Trump-Putin talks would take, though a Kremlin spokesperson indicated short informal talks may happen without large delegations in the room.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised fears of a plan to end the war being discussed in the absence of representatives from Kyiv or Europe.

Wednesday's handshake was the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since August 2025, when the Russian leader travelled to Alaska for talks on the Ukraine war which failed to deliver a breakthrough.
Xi's personal reception for Trump at the airport mimicked a similar move by the US president when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September, a gesture Xi described as "special".
A red carpet was rolled out in front of Air Force One for Trump, with a cheering crowd, honour guard, military flyover and flowers presentation all in place to welcome him.
Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua quoted Xi as saying he wanted to pursue a "constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality".
Xi's greeting will be seen as a diplomatic gesture designed to begin the week's talks with his American counterpart on a cordial note.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A lavish welcome ceremony was laid on for Trump's arrival

blocks.text: A lavish welcome ceremony was laid on for Trump's arrival
The Apec summit is being held in Shenzhen, south-east China, a booming for manufacturing and advanced tech.

It comes against the backdrop of the ousting of Nvidia chief executing Jensen Huang, who admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of spying for Beijing - a claim dismissed as a "smear" by China.
Trump has pursued warmer relations with China but the incident points to ongoing tensions between the two powers.
Several hours before Trump's arrival, Putin landed in Shenzhen and held around two hours of talks with Xi, with whom he has pressed for closer economic and defence relations.
Xi said both countries would "move forward steadily and boldly" and that the relationship was "stable as a mountain, unshaken by storms".

articles.title: First Thing: Peltola’s Alaska victory secures 56th Democratic seat in Senate
articles.summary:
The ninth gain of the midterms in the upper chamber, it is the first time Alaska has elected a Democrat since 2008. Plus the impact the NAZA documentary is having inside Israel

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. Democrats will control 56 seats in the upper chamber after the final Senate race was called in favor of Mary Peltola. The party gained nine Senate seats in the midterms, a sweeping victory that will put them decisively back in the majority beginning next year. Peltola, a former US House lawmaker, is the first Democrat Alaska has elected to the Senate since 2008.

Her campaign was dogged by controversy after the New York Times reported her staffers had helped recruit a second Republican challenger also named Dan Sullivan to run. Although Peltola’s team denied involvement, the alleged ruse prompted Donald Trump to call for her prosecution and triggered federal and state investigations.
National Security Agency network for internal communications goes down

The US National Security Agency said on Tuesday it had experienced “temporary degradation” during scheduled routine maintenance, after reports that its classified internal communications network had gone down. In a statement, the agency said some internal systems were affected but “mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational”.

The outage follows a run of technology failures in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop of flights, a Microsoft outage and disruption to banking services. None of those have been tied to a cyber-attack, though the causes of some have not been fully explained.

items: What has Marco Rubio said about the series of tech failures? The US secretary of state said: “We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind.”

Where have JD Vance and Sean Duffy tried to apportion blame? In separate interviews the vice-president and the transportation secretary have bizarrely tried to link Friday’s flight stoppage with transgender issues.

blocks.text: Biden criticizes Zelenskyy as ‘moody’ and ‘not as grateful as I expected’ in new memoir

blocks.caption: Joe Biden in a bilateral meeting with the president of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images

blocks.text: In a new memoir, Joe Biden offers harsh criticism of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has led Ukraine through four and a half years of war against Russia. According to Biden, the Ukrainian president was “difficult to work with”, “moody and stubborn in our private conversations”, and “not as grateful as I expected” for US diplomatic support and military aid.

items: How did Ukraine pull off the attack on the Kerch bridge, a symbol of Putin’s rule? Luke Harding reports from Kyiv on the in-depth preparations Ukraine made before launching a wave of attacks against the bridge that links Russia with occupied Crimea, personally opened by the Russian president in 2018.

How is Kyiv coping with continued Russian strikes? Many homes in Ukraine’s capital only have power for four hours a day, well before the winter months when freezing temperatures will put far more strain on infrastructure. Andrew Roth reports that many are beginning to blame the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, for failing to prepare.

blocks.text: Man armed with axe accused of destroying US military plane at Shannon airport in Ireland

blocks.caption: A US military C-130H aircraft. Photograph: US Department of Justice/PA

blocks.text: An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked at an Irish airport, US prosecutors claimed. Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks during the incident in April. He is not in US custody and his arraignment on the charge has not been scheduled.
Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang

blocks.caption: The former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Photograph: Ann Wang/Reuters

blocks.text: Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chair of the company’s board said during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster. Nvidia announced its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The announcement comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.
Isolated Brazilian tribe emerges amid alarm over threats to group’s way of life

blocks.caption: Young Awá men seen in 2017. Photograph: Scott Wallace/Getty Images

blocks.text: About 20 members of the uncontacted Awá Indigenous group emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, entering a village. Local people offered food to the group, who asked for yams before returning to the forest. With local Indigenous leaders warning of “clear signs of severe emaciation” among the children and elderly Awá, rights groups said the rare contact raised alarm over increasing incursions by illegal loggers, hunters and cattle ranchers into their territory.
In other news …

blocks.caption: Asif Merchant, a Pakistani man with alleged ties to Iran, appears on charges in connection with a foiled plot to assassinate Trump. Photograph: Jane Rosenberg/Reuters

items: A Pakistani man was sentenced to more than 27 years in prison for plotting to assassinate Donald Trump in retaliation for the US killing of the Revolutionary Guards commander Qassem Suleimani.

An eight-year-old Haitian boy has returned home to California after being released from ICE custody. The third-grader was put in restraints and taken into custody and held in Texas after a check-in earlier in the month.
The Costa Rican journalist Camilo Rodríguez has been shot dead. He had gained prominence for publishing allegations against ⁠suspected drug traffickers and politicians.

California prosecutors and victims’ advocates have sued the state’s governor to stop him from commuting death sentences. Gavin Newsom’s mass clemency action would leave all 548 people facing execution in the state instead facing life sentences without the possibility of parole.
The US has lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, global health authorities announced.
Amazon’s founder and billionaire chair Jeff Bezos has said he was “heavily involved” in the decision to cast Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

blocks.text: Stat of the day: US Pentagon fails ninth straight audit

blocks.caption: The Pentagon. Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Pentagon failed a financial audit for the ninth consecutive year, according to an inspector general ⁠report – but an official said a majority of its units passed for the first time.
Well Actually: An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavor, fiber and savings

blocks.caption: Eat all of your veg.  Composite: Guardian design;  Norman Posselt; Creativ Studio Heinemann; Jessica Peterson; Charles Wollertz/Getty Images

blocks.text: If you discard the peels, skins, stalks and seeds when consuming fruit and vegetables you are missing out on a lot of value. Rachel Dixon has this comprehensive guide of what to incorporate into your diet – and what to avoid.
Don’t miss this: ‘They want silence’: how the film NAZA is shaking Israel

blocks.caption: A mural in Israel initially targeting the directors of the NAZA documentary has been altered to read ‘heroes’ instead of ‘traitors’. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: The film’s material is shocking – it details the secret systems that have left tens of thousands of civilians dead and millions more homeless, displaced and injured in Gaza. Michael Segalov examines its impact within Israel.
Climate check: Fossil-fuel industry accused of violating Colorado law over not disclosing drilling chemicals

blocks.caption: Crews work at an oil and gas rig in Weld County, Colorado. Photograph: RJ Sangosti/The Denver Post via Getty Images

blocks.text: The fossil-fuel industry is violating Colorado law by not disclosing which chemicals it uses in drilling, a new analysis by the FracTracker Alliance non-profit alleges, and state records show it has used illegal or dangerous compounds while fracking.

items: Follow the latest from Cop31 with Ajit Niranjan on our live blog.

blocks.caption: The central building of the Brooklyn Public Library. Photograph: Roy Rochlin/Getty Images

blocks.text: Inflation and expanding services are drawing more people to public libraries, which are offering everything from books to job support and free activities.

articles.title: Xi, Putin meet in China, ahead of summit with Trump
articles.summary: China's President Xi Jinping on Wednesday pledged to stand up against trade protectionism, while his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin criticized Western sanctions as the two set the stage for a…

image.caption: In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping shake hands Wednesday prior to a meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. (Sergei Bobylyov/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

China's President Xi Jinping on Wednesday pledged to stand up against trade protectionism, while his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin criticized Western sanctions as the two set the stage for a high-stakes trilateral meeting with ‌U.S. President Donald Trump.
Other countries watch with great interest as leaders of 3 powers prepare to meet

They delivered their speeches at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, hours before Trump landed in China after meeting key regional allies in Manila this week.

Xi greeted Trump at the airport, reciprocating the U.S. president's gesture at Joint Base Andrews in September when they last met. They had a brief hug and a short exchange before walking along the red carpet to their motorcades.
The two will participate in an APEC group photo and attend a banquet with other leaders.

They will meet ​with Putin on the sidelines on Thursday and potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and the U.S. war ​with Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, AI and nuclear weapons.

The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union that formalized spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-Second World War order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries.
What to know about Canada and China's new trade pact
It has also ​unnerved some European and Asian capitals, who fear the world's greatest military powers will disregard their interests.
The Wall Street Journal, in an editorial, said it was "a sign of Mr. Trump’s mercurial foreign policy that the [summit] is creating more anxiety among allies than adversaries."

The Kremlin this week dismissed comparisons with the Yalta Conference as "games of political scientists," but said the meeting will have a major impact on global affairs. Beijing said the trilateral will promote world peace.

items: Carney to meet with Trump at APEC, says Canada's trade ties with China are not U.S. president's top concern
Canada and China announce new trade measures and cultural partnerships on Carney's 1st day in Shenzhen

blocks.text: In his opening address, Xi urged support for what he ⁠called "free and open trade," trying to portray his ⁠country as a stable partner on the global stage, in contrast with the U.S., which has raised tariffs and ‌adopted a more muscular foreign policy under Trump.

Xi's remarks came after Washington announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, which could further complicate a fragile trade truce with Beijing. China has pledged to retaliate.

"We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains," Xi told an audience of business executives.
Dancers wave Russian and Chinese flags during the welcoming ceremony for Putin on Wednesday. (Anupam Nath/The Associated Press)
Western trade partners have ⁠criticized China for running annual trade surpluses exceeding $1 trillion US through policies that support its manufacturing sector at the expense of its consumers.

Beijing says its growth model is appropriate for an economy still catching up with the world's richest, but the U.S., the European Union in Brussels and others are concerned about China's supply chain dominance providing the country with geopolitical leverage and say its policies threaten their industries and jobs.

Xi said China will continue to invest in its industrial complex and ‌develop new technologies that would also benefit other countries. The world's second-largest economy will lower tariffs and further open up its markets, while standing up against protectionism and unilateralism, he added.

His "message is likely to resonate with many Global South countries and reinforces Beijing's effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group.

items: How China is positioning itself as a global leader as it hosts Trump, Putin
Ukraine cripples Crimean bridge in blow to Putin before meeting with Xi, Trump

blocks.text: Trump's trip to Asia is his first since his Republican Party's defeat in midterm elections, while allegations involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy ​add to the tension.

Trump has downplayed the allegations, having developed a close relationship with Huang over the past two years, and both he and his Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have faced questions over when they knew about the allegations, given weighty decisions that were made by the White House over export controls on Nvidia chips.

items: No plans to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia chair tells investors
What the Jensen Huang scandal means for Trump and his administration

blocks.text: Most analysts expect Washington and Beijing to keep ties relatively stable as Trump and Xi are set to follow their meeting in Shenzhen with their fourth of the year at the Group of 20 gathering in Miami in December.

Putin, who was speaking after ⁠Ukraine crippled the vital Kerch road bridge linking Crimea to Russia in a major blow to his four-year-old war, followed Xi on stage with a speech that described Western powers as "former hegemons."
U.S. President Donald Trump and Xi applaud as the U.S. leader arrives at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on Wednesday. (Mandel Ngan/Getty Images)
He said Europe ⁠was in a "humiliating decline" and that anti-Russian sanctions imposed after his invasion of Ukraine had backfired.
"Experience has shown that the traditional tools of economic dominance and de facto coercion have largely run their ⁠course, having lost much ⁠of their intimidating power," Putin said.
"While sanctions, tariffs, and export restrictions ​may still exert a certain deterrent effect, they are incapable of halting growth — let alone crushing the economies of competitors."
Ukraine's strike on Putin's bridge carries symbolic weight. Will it change the war?
Putin described the world as "turbulent" but said disagreements can be addressed by "sitting at the table."
"I therefore expect big potential benefit from the upcoming trilateral meeting," he said.
On Tuesday, Taiwan and Japan flagged incursions by Russian aircraft into their airspace.
In a bilateral meeting later, Xi and Putin praised their close partnership and pledged more measures that advance ​a "multipolar world."

In Manila, Trump vowed to deepen defence co-operation ⁠with the Philippines, amid its growing friction with Beijing over disputed features in the South China Sea. Earlier, he floated the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, but that has not been confirmed.
With files from CBC News

articles.summary: 'Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,' House Speaker Bojie Dy tells ASEAN parliamentarians

blocks.text: ADDRESS. House Speaker Bojie Dy delivers a speech at the opening ceremony of the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly General Assembly in Manila on November 18, 2026.
AIPA Philippines 2026 on Facebook
'Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,' House Speaker Bojie Dy tells ASEAN parliamentarians

items: The ASEAN parliamentary body is increasingly concerned about the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and the need for a collaborative regional approach to address its challenges.
While the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly can influence member states to adopt regional commitments, any resolutions passed are non-binding and cannot enforce legislation.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The persistent threat of artificial intelligence (AI) is a cloud hanging over the parliamentary body of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but uncertainty remains over any concrete measure to approach the subject.

“It’s a concern for everybody, it’s a growing concern, and I think it cannot be addressed by one country. It has to be a concerted effort among the regions and other countries to be able to make sure that this is not abused,” House Senior Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez, head of the Philippine delegation for the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly, said on the sidelines of the AIPA on Wednesday, November 18.

“Artificial intelligence is advancing faster than many of our laws can keep pace with. No single parliament can manage these challenges alone,” House Speaker Bojie Dy, current AIPA president, also said in his opening speech.
Hernandez, however, sidestepped questions about whether a resolution on AI was being drafted during the AIPA general assembly, but said any effort will be “patterned on what transpired in the ASEAN.”

In 2025, the ASEAN adopted a declaration in Kuala Lumpur establishing an ASEAN AI Safety Network, a regional mechanism aimed at promoting collaboration among member states and addressing cross-border AI risks.

AIPA, as a regional parliamentary bloc, is not as powerful as the European Parliament. Any resolution passed during the general assembly is non-binding, which means it cannot force member parliaments to pass legislation back home.
AIPA, however, can still exercise influence by encouraging member parliaments to adopt regional commitments in their own countries.

Concerns about AI come as the Philippines’ hosting of ASEAN was met with massive protests against the US-led initiative Pax Silica, which will lead to the construction of a 1600-hectare AI industrial hub in New Clark City. The project is feared to displace hundreds of indigenous peoples and farmers, according to Human Rights Watch.
Only Singapore and the Philippines are ASEAN signatories to the Pax Silica initiative so far. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us
articles.summary: Is keeping a family business together always worth the cost?

blocks.text: What happens when the people you inherited a business with are also the people you can no longer work with? You can quit a job, sell your shares, or find a new business partner. But what if that partner is your brother, sister, cousin, or parent, and the company is something your grandparents spent their lives building?

I have covered Philippine business families for most of my journalism career, interviewing relatives locked in battles over ownership, leadership, inheritance, and family land. Some disputes were already playing out in court, while others were waged quietly behind closed boardroom doors even as the companies kept running. As the feud between cousins Federico “Piki” Lopez and Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III unfolded this year, I found myself returning to those stories, my interview notes, and reading Harvard Business Review research on why family businesses fight and how some survive. In June, I joined family-business adviser Enrique Soriano in an online forum with business owners across Asia to discuss why even wildly successful dynasties break apart.

The Lopez cousins are hardly the first wealthy family to face this problem. India’s Ambani brothers split up the Reliance empire their father built, while the Ortigases fought over control of their real estate business. In Singapore, a father accused his son of trying to take over the board of one of the country’s biggest property developers. Some families eventually called a truce. Others decided they could no longer be business partners, and still fought for years, burning through cash on lawyers and leaving the next generation to clean up the mess.
All of this brought me back to one big question: Is keeping a family business together always worth the cost?

For decades, the Lopez name has been tied to some of the Philippines’ most famous companies: ABS-CBN, Meralco, Benpres (now Lopez Holdings), First Philippine Holdings, First Gen, and Rockwell Land. The businesses changed over time, yet the family stayed connected to an empire their elders built, lost, won back, and rebuilt.

Under Oscar Lopez‘s leadership, the family published Phoenix, a book about how they bounced back from hard times. Piki wanted a different symbol for the next chapter: not the phoenix, which rises again after being destroyed, but the butterfly, which transforms into something completely new. He has also talked a lot about compounding, the idea that smart decisions made consistently over decades pay off far more than quick wins. In his September speeches to stockholders, he stressed that “direction matters more than speed,” pointing to the group’s decision ten years earlier to stop building coal-fired power plants even when coal was still making good money.

That mindset explains Piki’s game plan for First Gen’s energy investments. He believes the company must prepare for a power market that relies more and more on renewable energy. His cousins have questioned whether the bets he’s making are worth the massive price tag, risks, and years of waiting. They have also challenged his authority to make those calls on his own. Gabby and his allied cousins wanted something very different: immediate cash flow and shared family stewardship over a distressed media mission—ABS-CBN—that could not afford to wait until 2031 for long-gestation hydro projects to pay off.

blocks.caption: EXCLUSIVE: Inside Piki Lopez’s town hall as cousins rally for ABS-CBN

blocks.text: The fight turned public and personal. In April, majority owners of Lopez Inc.—representing three of the four branches of the family—accused Piki of acting “like a king without accountability,” questioning First Gen’s deals with Enrique Razon Jr.’s Prime Infrastructure, including selling control of its natural-gas business and investing in water-pumping hydropower projects. The majority group later called the hydropower bet “a horrible deal.” First Gen pushed back on those claims, defending the business logic, pricing, and board approvals behind its deals.

The cousins reached a ceasefire in May, but it didn’t hold, and by August, Gabby’s branch sold its 25.68% share in Lopez Inc., the private holding company sitting at the very top of the family empire, to businessman Ramon Ang for about P11.56 billion. Meanwhile, ABS-CBN lined up fresh funding. Piki then locked down control of the boards of Lopez Holdings and First Philippine Holdings (FPH), the two companies that hold the group’s stakes in First Gen and geothermal giant Energy Development Corporation (EDC). In November, FPH approved the proposed P15.92-billion sale of its 90.74% controlling stake in Rockwell Land to Gabby’s branch’s investment firm, Crème Investment Corporation, a deal that is still waiting to close. (READ: What it took to save ABS-CBN)
Taken together, these deals suggest the cousins are moving toward a future where they no longer have to agree on how to run the same businesses.
But is splitting up actually better than staying together?

One family owner wants bigger cash payouts today, while the relative running the company wants to plow back those profits into growing the business. Another thinks they should sell the company while buyers are offering a good price, while someone else wants to save it for the grandkids. One wants to ride out an industry slump, convinced a struggling business will bounce back, while another wants to stop pouring money into what looks like a sinking ship, especially when that cash could fund a different business that takes years of heavy spending before turning a profit.

Yet each walks away believing the others are greedy, reckless, or unreasonable. The real trouble starts when the people around the boardroom table aren’t just ordinary investors, but siblings who grew up competing for their parents’ and uncles’ attention, cousins who feel their branch of the family sacrificed more, or heirs who remember the founder’s wishes differently.

Josh Baron and Rob Lachenauer, who advise business families and write for Harvard Business Review, explain how everyday business arguments turn deeply personal. In Why Fights Erupt in Family Businesses, they show how fights over money, power, and status get tangled up with family history. An argument over company spending can bring back old resentment over unequal treatment. A fight over who gets to be CEO can reopen old arguments about favoritism. Selling a company might look like a smart opportunity to one relative and a betrayal of the family legacy to another.

Soriano raised another complication during our webinar: many family businesses stay united for decades simply because one strong founder or family elder can settle all the arguments. Relatives might not like every decision, yet they accept the leader’s authority. Once that leader passes away, the next generation realizes it has inherited not only the businesses, but also old disagreements that were never truly resolved.

The Lopezes had larger-than-life leaders in Eugenio “Geny” Lopez Jr. and his brother Oscar, who died in 1999 and 2023, leaving their successors to figure out how to own and run surviving empires without those strong elders around to settle arguments.
Other Philippine families have ended up in far messier wars.

Take Banco Filipino, once the country’s biggest savings bank, famous for its slogan, “Subok na Matibay, Subok na Matatag (Tested Strong, Proven Stable).” Founded by Tomas Aguirre in 1964, the bank was shut down by the Central Bank in January 1985 before reopening in 1994 after the Supreme Court ruled the Central Bank had abused its power. But its headaches were far from over. It kept clashing with regulators over financial aid, its money troubles, and the fallout from its first shutdown.

blocks.caption: BANCO FILIPINO. This spread in Newsbreak’s March 3, 2003 issue shows the late Don Tomas Aguirre (left) and his children, Ana Marie Aguirre-Koruga (upper right), and Albert “Bobby” Aguirre (bottom right) on a polo field. Rappler

blocks.text: At the same time, the Aguirre family was tearing itself apart from the inside. I covered the legal fight involving Ana Maria Aguirre-Koruga, a minority stockholder who sued the bank’s directors in 2003, including her own brother, Albert Aguirre, who was then vice chairman. She accused them of risky banking practices, conflicts of interest, and shady loans meant to enrich insiders. The directors denied the claims. In 2009, the Supreme Court ruled in Koruga v. Arcenas that her complaints belonged with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), not a regular trial court. That ruling only decided who had authority to hear the case, not whether her accusations were true. The bank shut down for good on March 17, 2011, under BSP orders. The state deposit insurer, Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation, took over a bank with 62 branches, 173,480 accounts, and P17.8 billion in customer deposits. The family and regulators kept arguing over who was to blame. While the sibling feud wasn’t the sole reason Banco Filipino collapsed—its financial and regulatory problems ran much deeper—the family war played out inside a bank holding the life savings of thousands of ordinary Filipinos.

The Ilusorio family feud got even more personal. Potenciano “Nanoy” Ilusorio built a multi-billion-peso empire anchored by prime real estate, the pioneering satellite firm Philcomsat, and the exclusive Baguio Country Club. But by 1999, his six children had split into rival camps over their parents, the family fortune, and who should be in charge. When Nanoy grew old and frail, some of his children took him under their care, prompting their mother, Erlinda Kalaw-Ilusorio, to sue them for allegedly keeping her husband away from her, a battle the Supreme Court dismissed in 2001 as the “sad tale of a prominent family shattered by conflicts on expectancy in fabled fortune.” (READ: What drives people to declare war against their own flesh and blood?)

Even Nanoy’s death in June that year didn’t stop nearly 300 civil and criminal lawsuits filed between the rival camps, and according to an account Soriano published in 2016, some children only found out of Erlinda’s death four days later, leading to separate funerals. At one service, the urn reportedly held Nanoy’s ashes because another branch of the family kept Erlinda’s. Another service reportedly barred three of the sisters at the door with security guards.
A fight that started over money and power had reached the point where children could not even mourn their parents together.

In other prominent Philippine clans, the fracture began not at a parent’s deathbed, but when siblings began questioning how a brother or sister was managing inherited assets—turning boardroom suspicions into criminal complaints and proxy wars.

For the Jacintos, who built their wealth in steel, banking, and real estate, also fought over their inheritance. After their patriarch, Fernando Jacinto died, his children clashed over how family properties were being managed and sold. Musician and businessman Ramon “RJ” Jacinto stepped in after relatives questioned real estate deals handled by their sister Marilene, who was running parts of the family business. One fight centered on a large property in Misamis Oriental sold in 2007 for P226 million, which RJ’s camp argued was far below its appraised value. Another involved a Novaliches property reportedly worth about P300 million. Acting as president of family-owned Oregon Land Inc., RJ accused Marilene of faking a deed to transfer the land. Prosecutors charged her in 2012 with falsifying public documents, an accusation that led to criminal proceedings, though not a conviction. The feud showed how inheritance fights can quickly spiral into claims of betrayal and criminal charges between brothers and sisters. (READ: Shaping the future: Family legacies)

blocks.caption: Family feud: Court ruling saves Olivia Yanson’s share in PH’s biggest transport fleet

blocks.text: In the Yanson family, the trigger was a boardroom ouster over who would run the business. They parents founded Vallacar Transit Inc. and the Ceres bus empire, considered among the largest bus conglomerates in Southeast Asia with about 5,000 buses ferrying 700,000 to 850,000 passengers in routes across Visayas and Mindanao regions. In July 2019, four siblings—Roy, Emily, Ricardo Jr., and Ma. Lourdes Celina Yanson-Lopez—tried to oust their youngest brother, Leo Rey Yanson, from running the bus group. Their mother, Olivia Yanson, sided with Leo Rey and Ginette, splitting the family into Yanson 4 and Yanson 2 camps. They fought over who had the right to elect board directors and run the company, triggering lawsuits and battles over company records. In 2025, the Supreme Court said Olivia was mentally sound when she executed her will that designated the Yanson 2 camp as the righful heirs of their family business empire. The family still hasn’t reached the kind of broad peace deal needed to put the feud behind them. (READ: Yanson family feud gets uglier as court brands 4 siblings ‘fugitives from justice’)

This family drama resonated elsewhere in Asia where South Korea’s Lotte Group—the retail, hospitality, and confectionery giant behind Asia’s largest department stores, luxury hotels, and iconic snacks—became the stage for a succession war between brothers Shin Dong-joo and Shin Dong-bin, sons of founder Shin Kyuk-ho. The business giant had major operations in both Japan and South Korea. Dong-joo, the older brother, was prominent in Japan, while Dong-bin ran much of the Korean side. After Dong-joo lost top posts in Japan in late 2014 and early 2015, the brothers erupted into a public war over who had their father’s blessing and who should lead the empire. Their elderly father was pulled straight into the crossfire. At one point, Shin Kyuk-ho backed his eldest son, prompting Dong-bin’s camp to question whether their father was still mentally fit to make decisions. The brothers battled through shareholder votes, lawsuits, and press statements, turning their father’s mental health and legal guardianship into a court case. Dong-bin eventually won over shareholders and kept control, though Dong-joo kept fighting him. Instead of splitting the empire in two, one brother walked away with control of the main group.

blocks.caption: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

blocks.text: The Shin feud proved a hard truth: being the founder’s son, even being the oldest, doesn’t guarantee inheriting the throne.

In Singapore, the Kwek family— the powers behind iconic skyscrapers, luxury condos, and over 160 hotels worldwide—showed how quickly a disagreement between a father and son could move from the family boardroom into the headlines. In February 2025, City Developments executive chairman Kwek Leng Beng accused his son, chief executive Sherman Kwek, of attempting a boardroom “coup” by bypassing governance rules to appoint independent directors, prompting the elder Kwek to go to court to fire his son. Trading in City Developments shares was suspended as the confrontation became public. For a listed property developer, the dispute raised questions that went beyond the relationship between father and son: Who had the authority to appoint directors? Were corporate procedures being followed? And could the company continue operating effectively while its chairman and chief executive were fighting?

Yet the confrontation ended relatively quickly. On March 12, 2025, City Developments announced that the court proceedings had been settled and would be discontinued. Kwek Leng Beng remained executive chairman and Sherman remained chief executive, while the two newly appointed independent directors whose appointments had sparked the dispute, Jennifer Duong Young and Wong Su-Yen, stepped down. Singapore’s Straits Times later reported that trusted family friends and senior figures had helped mediate the truce. The company continued under the same family leadership, although the settlement did not necessarily mean that every personal disagreement had been resolved.

Here in the Philippines, the Ortigas family—the landed dynasty behind Ortigas Center and Greenhills—also managed to save its core property business after years of infighting. At stake was OCLP Holdings, which controls prime Ortigas land, Greenhills Shopping Center, and Tiendesitas. To gain an edge, rival branches teamed up with competing giants: the Rafael Ortigas group with Ayala Land, and the Francisco Ortigas group with SM Prime Holdings. The battle spilled into court over board elections and whether nominees tied to a rival developer could hold seats.

Those divisions let Ayala and SM deepen their footholds in a fractured enterprise. In November 2014, the developers and Ortigas factions dropped their lawsuits and agreed to work together. The family kept its landholdings intact rather than carving them up, though peace came at a steep price: bringing in powerful giants handed outsiders major influence over an empire that had belonged to the Ortigas family for generations.

There are strong business reasons to keep a family group intact. Companies under common ownership can share cash, talent, bank relationships, and leadership, allowing a stronger sister company to help a struggling one survive a rough patch or undertake massive investments too large for one branch alone. There is also the pull of family history, where a business built by a grandfather means far more to his grandkids than an ordinary stock investment, making a sale feel like erasing part of the family identity even when the financial math makes sense.
Yet keeping a company together merely because the founder wanted it kept together can create another problem: What happens when the next generation no longer agrees on what the business should do?

Adviser Josh Baron has argued in Why Family Businesses Need to Find the Right Level of Conflict that avoiding disagreement is actually unhealthy. Families must debate tough questions rather than letting owners quietly stew over decisions they feel powerless to change. When relatives can still negotiate and compromise, staying together preserves huge value. But when every investment, dividend payout, job appointment, or asset sale becomes another war for control, the cost becomes far too high.
India’s Ambani family decided that the brothers were simply better off running different companies. (READ: Timeline: Key dates in India’s Ambani brothers’ dispute)

After founder Dhirubhai Ambani died in 2002 without leaving a will, his sons Mukesh and Anil fought publicly over who would control Reliance Industries—India’s largest private-sector conglomerate, spanning petrochemicals, refining, telecom, and retail—until their mother, Kokilaben, stepped in to broker a June 2005 peace deal. Mukesh kept Reliance Industries and its core oil and chemical operations, while Anil took charge of telecom, power, and financial services. But it didn’t stop every argument as the brothers later fought over natural-gas supply deals in a battle that reached India’s Supreme Court. Still, they no longer had to agree on every single investment or management call.

India’s Bajaj family—one of the country’s oldest business dynasties, famous for putting India on wheels as a motorcycle, scooter, and financial services powerhouse—also split up its companies among different branches after years of fighting. Under a 2008 settlement, Shishir Bajaj’s branch took control of businesses like Bajaj Hindusthan and Bajaj Consumer Care, while other family branches kept the group’s core auto, finance, and industrial companies.

blocks.caption: Why the Lopez cousins are breaking up — and what other feuding dynasties teach us

blocks.text: Splitting up let each branch follow its own game plan. Their paths quickly diverged: the core Bajaj businesses boomed, while Bajaj Hindusthan struggled with heavy debt and a tough sugar market. Dividing the empire ended the fight over who was in charge, but it didn’t guarantee that both sides would win.

In Hong Kong, Walter Kwok was pushed out as leader of Sun Hung Kai Properties—the real estate titan behind the city’s tallest skyscrapers, luxury malls, and housing estates—in 2008 after clashing with his brothers Thomas and Raymond over how to run the empire. The battle pulled in their mother, Kwong Siu-hing, and tangled up the family trusts. Walter lost his executive job, though he didn’t lose his financial slice of the family fortune. He went on to start his own property company, Empire Group Holdings, while new trust rules spelled out each brother’s share of the family wealth.

Taking a different path is the Murdoch family—the real-life inspiration behind HBO’s hit drama Succession, and the media dynasty behind Fox News, The Wall Street Journal, and major outlets across the US, UK, and Australia that have shaped elections and public debate for decades. After a court battle over the family trust controlling voting power in Fox Corporation and News Corp, a September 2025 settlement locked in Lachlan Murdoch’s future control. His three older siblings from 95-year-old Rupert Murdoch‘s first two marriages—Prudence MacLeod, Elisabeth Murdoch, and James Murdoch—walked away with huge payouts and exited the trust. Grace and Chloe, Murdoch’s two youngest daughters from his third wife, Wendi Deng, stayed on as financial beneficiaries under the new setup, but without the voting power given to Lachlan.

Each of these families handled their split differently. The Ambanis and Bajajs divided up operating companies. Walter Kwok stepped out of management while keeping a financial stake. The Murdochs rewrote who holds voting control over their media empire. None of them offers a one-size-fits-all recipe for solving family feuds.

blocks.caption: ADVICE. Enrique Soriano, family business consultant of the Wong & Bernstein  Group, speaks during a forum. Courtesy of the Wong & Bernstein Group

blocks.text: Enrique Soriano, who has advised business families across the Philippines and Asia, does not view such separations as failures, noting during our June webinar that relatives who can no longer work together are often better served by an orderly division of business interests so they can stop being business partners without stopping being family.

Of course, that is much easier said than done. A family deciding to split still has to agree on who gets what, how much each company is worth, who takes on the debts, and what happens to shared properties. One relative might want out, only to find the others can’t afford to buy their shares. Another might want to keep control, but has to bring in an outside investor to help pay for the buyout.
And a peace deal that satisfies the relatives doesn’t automatically work out for the everyday public investors who also have money riding on those companies.

The Lopez cousins appear to be heading toward a more permanent split of their business interests, though whether that turns out well for their companies, outside stockholders, and the family itself will take years to see.
Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled itPart 2 | Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN strugglesPart 3 | Why Piki Lopez is letting Rockwell go

Other business dynasties offer no easy answers: The Kweks and Ortigases found ways to keep their shared businesses intact after fierce battles, though both had to make major compromises. The Ambanis and Bajajs carved up their empires. The Kwoks and Murdochs separated day-to-day control from financial ownership. The Shin brothers’ succession war left one brother running Lotte, while the Aguirres, Ilusorios, Jacintos, and Yansons showed how family fights can spiral into years of lawsuits and lasting broken relationships and personal wounds.

There is a world of difference between keeping a company together because the owners actually agree on its future, and keeping it together just because nobody wants to be blamed for breaking up the family empire. There is also a difference between splitting up to chase new ambitions and splitting it up just to stop a fight.

For the Lopezes, going their separate ways may give each branch the freedom to focus on what it values most. Piki can concentrate on long-term energy bets, while Gabby and his allies can focus on lifestyle-related consumer and media businesses. Yet, that freedom brings new pressures, and success will depend on the choices each side makes next.

A family can survive a corporate divorce. Its companies might even grow stronger because of it. Or the split could leave both sides worse off than before. But the real question isn’t just whether relatives should stay together or go their separate ways. It is whether the businesses, and all the people who depend on them, will actually be better off afterward. – Rappler.com
Part 2 on Thursday, November 19 | Dividing the Lopez empire: Who decides what a family business is worth?Part 3 on Friday, November 20 | Two cousins, two big bets: Will the Lopez split actually work?

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.
