articles.title: Shabana Mahmood pledges to tackle ‘corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing’ – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Home secretary to give speech to National Police Chiefs’ Council addressing concerns that officers treats groups differently

Good morning. Shabana Mahmood has done two of…

blocks.text: Good morning. Shabana Mahmood has done two of the most difficult jobs in the government. With Labour under pressure from anti-migrant populists, in Reform UK, in the Conservative party and in the media, as justice secretary and home secretary she has been on the frontline in all the debates where the fight between the right and progressive politics has been most intensive. And she has developed a bold, novel, and largely successful strategy for winning these battles; she disarms her critics by agreeing with them.
Not entirely, of course. She is still a Labour cabinet minister. But sometimes she can sound a bit like Chris Philp.

And today we are going to get another example. In a speech to the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC), she will tell officers that she wants to do something about so-called two-tier policing – the theory that, under pressure to be politically correct, the police have become biased towards leftwing causes and nervous about enforcing the law against minority ethnic people for fear of being seen as racist.

On the right, the existence of this version of two-tier policing is now an article of faith, even though most of the time actual policing is very different. This is how Robert Hutton from the Critic satirised the idea in a sketch two years ago, during 2024 summer riots when racists were trying to burn down hotels housing asylum seekers.

double quotation markThis is about fairness, Ed, and it’s a very important point. When I talk about two-tier policing, I’m talking about the way that different groups of marchers are treated. For instance, if you go to a Pride march, there are police with rainbow flags on their cars. During the Black Lives Matter protests, the police took the knee. But you go to these protests, and do you see the police waving swastikas? No you don’t. When was the last time you saw a film of a policeman kicking a brown-skinned person in the head? Well, OK, but when was the last time you saw a video of a policeman trying to set fire to a building full of refugees? Exactly. That’s what we mean by two-tier policing.

Here is a Guardian article looking at whether policing really is two-tier. In some respects, it is, the article points out. “Black people remained more likely than any other ethnic group to be subjected to almost every form of force, from handcuffing and dog bites to firearms and Tasers, when compared with population or arrest figures.”

In her speech today, from the extracts released in advance, Mahmood is not going to say that there is two-tier policing. But she will argue that it is important to respond to the “perception” it exists. She will say:

double quotation markWe must tackle head-on the corrosive and growing perception of two-tier policing in this country. Now let me be clear: I know the vast majority of officers police impartially and that policing without fear or favour is their creed. But there have been examples of differential treatment and they have harmed policing, allowing people – often motivated actors – to whip up the idea that there is two-tier policing in this country.
In its report previewing the speech, the Press Association says:

double quotation markMahmood will lament the low levels of black officers in police forces, while also warning against “misguided attempts at course correction” that lead to “differential treatment”. And she will warn officers against engaging with “activist groups”, telling them to “leave the politics to the politicians”. She will also set out plans to fast-track talented recruits – including from outside policing – to senior ranks to address sometimes “inadequate” leadership. A new “impartiality standard” is being developed to ensure all members of the public are treated equally, she will tell chief constables and police and crime commissioners. This will bring guidance on key impartiality principles into one place and aims to give police more confidence in how they handle cases, regardless of someone’s race, faith or other characteristics, and to give the public confidence they will be treated fairly. A third of Britons believe police treat people from ethnic minority backgrounds more favourably than white people, a More in Common poll found earlier this year, noting this marks a doubling in the last two years. Mahmood will tell the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) that it is “shameful”, 33 years after the murder of black teenager Stephen Lawrence, that the proportion of black officers remains virtually unchanged. But Mahmood will argue that some approaches intended to promote equality, such as the former police anti-racism commitment, have risked undermining confidence in impartial policing.
Mahmood will say:

double quotation markWe must also be wary of misguided attempts at course correction, where the pursuit of equality leads instead to differential treatment. To the public, it was patently absurd to tell police officers that fair policing does not mean treating everyone the same.

This is a reference to the Police Anti-Racism Commitment, a document that has frequently been criticised by the Conservatives and Reform UK. It says producing equality of policing outcomes “does not mean treating everyone ‘the same’”.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.30am: Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, gives evidence to the Commons Northern Ireland committee.
11am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, gives a speech at the King’s Fund conference.
Noon: Andy Burnham faces Kemi Badenoch at PMQs.
1pm: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, gives a speech on policing.
After 12.30pm: MPs begin a debate on a Tory opposition day motion opposing most of the key features of the PM’s proposed UK-EU reset deal due to be agreed on Friday.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: How a green economy could help reverse climate change
articles.summary: Green growth promises a future in which economies thrive without destroying the environment. But is this vision realistic?

image.caption: 'Business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies': is this the way to a greener future?Image: Ian Grant/Design Pics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Human civilization is currently profoundly unsustainable. Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries critical for sustaining life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity.
If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.

It's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change. That's where the idea of green growth comes in.

Its promise is to keep growing the economy while reducing emissions and resource use. That involves, for instance, running factories, businesses and homes on wind, solar and other green energy instead of coal and gas, replacing gas-fired furnaces with heat pumps and recycling and reusing resources and raw materials.

"Basically, the idea is: business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies," said Helmut Haberl, a social ecology professor at BOKU University in Vienna. Along with his colleagues in 2020, he published a major report evaluating more than 800 studies on green growth.

blocks.caption: Will running economies on renewable energy be enough to completely prevent environmental damage from economic growth?Image: Wang Shengwei/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Can economies grow while emissions fall?

In principle, the world's economic output could continue to grow in the long term and generate significantly fewer emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. That's been shown in scenarios modeled by researchers with the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC.
Thanks to renewable energy and green technologies, those scenarios have already become reality in several countries and regions.

The economies of developed countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan and Australia have experienced years of growth alongside sinking CO2 emissions. That's even when offshored production is included.
In the European Union, the bloc-wide economy has grown by more than 70% since 1990. Meanwhile, the EU's carbon emissions have dropped by around 40%.
But such a complete decoupling of growth and emissions is, according to Haberl and his fellow researchers, relatively rare.

In India, and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, economies are becoming more efficient. But while economic performance is outpacing emissions growth, emissions are still rising in those countries and globally. This is not compatible with preventing the worst impacts of climate change.
"That doesn't mean, however, that it couldn't work in the future," said Haberl, referring to decoupling of growth and emissions.
And even though economic growth has been shown to be compatible with emissions reduction, eliminating all greenhouse gases from a polluting industry like steel or chemicals is complicated.
These sectors don't just release emissions by burning fossil fuels for energy; carbon is also a key part of the chemical processes used to create their products, notably in the steel industry.
Replacing it with greener substitutes, or an alternative energy source like green hydrogen, requires significant investment.
Emissions aren't the only problem with economic growth

There's another hurdle: the world's high consumption of resources. A productive economy depends on many raw materials and other products: ores, chemicals, wood, cement, glass and agricultural products.
EU Arctic strategy highlights security and raw materials
Many countries are now using green technologies to reduce the amount of resources needed to manufacture a product, for example, and are making their economies more efficient.

But that doesn't mean that overall fewer resources are being used, because falling costs can encourage businesses to produce more things and people to consume more. This can partially offset green savings and is called the rebound effect.
The British economy has been growing for years, emissions have been dropping and efficiency has increased — but the UK still used 7% more resources in 2023 than it did in 2001.

Global consumption of resources has tripled over the last 50 years. If the world continues on the current pathway, that could increase by another 60% by 2060. It remains unclear green growth can deliver the emissions and resource reductions needed to stop climate change and biodiversity loss rapidly enough.

"We really need to move beyond efficiency gains in our existing production practices to look more broadly at what we consume," said Catherine Ganzleben, a sustainability and fair transitions expert at the European Environment Agency.

blocks.caption: Some 75 million new cars — including Volkswagens, seen here at a plant in Essen, Germany — are sold worldwide each yearImage: Martin Meissner/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: She told DW that people also need to reconsider how they consume and whether they really need to own everything they use in their daily life — cars, for example.
"But we can shift towards models where we share cars, so we pool our resources and have significantly lower resources per person through sharing the goods that we need."
Is degrowth the future?
Some researchers have come to the conclusion that unrestricted economic growth is no longer possible in the long term, even if it's sustainable.

Instead, they've called for degrowth. This posits slower economic growth, no growth at all or even negative growth, so that the world's ecosystems and the climate have a chance to recover and stabilize.

That applies mainly to economies in richer countries, which would need to take targeted steps to reduce their energy and resource use. Poorer countries would continue to grow until their economies and quality of life are significantly improved.

Under the degrowth theory, a society's prosperity is not measured solely by the growth of its gross domestic product, but by values such as quality of life, education and community. The idea is that once countries develop to a certain point, additional growth doesn't translate into greater well-being.

Ultimately, the concept is based on the idea that human well-being and ecological sustainability is only possible in the long term with a planned, socially just reduction of material production and resource consumption. Degrowth advocates argue this would be preferable to an unplanned and potentially catastrophic economic contraction caused by escalating climate extremes.
Degrowth: Slowing growth for the environment?

A 2020 study by researchers from the universities of Leeds and Lausanne showed that the concept of degrowth supported the world's climate goals — and that a high quality of life didn't have to be sacrificed in exchange for a significantly lower consumption of energy and resources.
However, there is still no conclusive evidence that a entire modern economy could continue to function entirely on the degrowth principles in the long term.
Is an environmentally friendly economy possible?
Nevertheless, Haberl doesn't assume that an environmentally friendly economic model automatically goes hand in hand with sacrifice, arguing instead in favor of a needs-based economy.

"A society isn't necessarily better off when it's producing more goods and services," he said. It all depends on how prosperity and quality of life are measured in the future, and how states decide to do business.

Today, a successful economy is measured by the growth of a country's gross domestic product — put simply, the worth of all of its goods and services. This calculation doesn't take into account income distribution, unpaid work, quality of life and environmental damage.

"The highest possible real incomes for every individual would probably not be compatible with ecological goals in the long term," said Haberl. "On the other hand, an increase in prosperity — related to a higher quality of life — would be."
Pitfalls of GDP — When growth isn't everything

An analysis by the European Environment Agency (EEA) pointed out that the idea of steady growth is part of the world's economic cycle, and deeply anchored in our institutions, norms and societal discourse. The job market and tax system are also closely tied to the growth of the gross domestic product. A shrinking economy would therefore require a fundamental shift in our way of thinking.

Countries are faced with a dilemma: a steadily growing economy is not compatible with ecological goals, according to the EEA. On the other side, a sharp decline in growth could trigger enormous social upheaval.

And the correlation is much more complex than the idea of "less is more," as highlighted by an EEA study in November 2021. "The fact that GDP growth has been harmful for the environment does not necessarily mean that declining GDP would be good for the environment," noted the report.

Achieving green growth while respecting environmental limits would require an "unprecedented decoupling of economic activity from environmental and climate pressures. Whether this is feasible is currently uncertain."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Fatal police shootings in Nunavik shattered trust. Can these new intervention teams help?
articles.summary: Saqijuq's Mobile Intervention Team (MIT) in Kuujjuaq is pairing intervention workers with officers in an effort to reduce police involvement, arrests and use of force. It comes on the heels of years…

image.caption: Ariane Richard, the co-ordinator of Saqijuq's Mobile Intervention Team (MIT) says her goal is to bring softness to interventions. When not on call, the MIT unit focuses on prevention and building connections by participating in local events, from karaoke and volleyball to trick-or-treating. (Rachel

blocks.text: The sun is nearly set by the time Ariane Richard starts her shift in Kuujjuaq, a village in northern Quebec.
And on an evening in early November, her back seat is full — with a police officer, a new intervention worker in training and a CBC News team, in tow.
After six years working in the North as an intervention worker, Richard says she's seen a lot.
"A lot of stuff you're not necessarily ready to see," she said.
But her newest role is a bit different.

For the past year, she's co-ordinated Saqijuq's Mobile Intervention Team (MIT) and led the unit in Kuujjuaq — pairing intervention workers with officers in an effort to reduce police involvement, arrests and use of force.

Established in the northern Quebec communities of Puvirnituq, Kuujjuaq and most recently Salluit, the Inuit-led organization says the team is meant to address pressing issues: suicide prevention, intimate partner violence, mental health crises and at-risk children.
The unit takes on interventions that require time, sensitivity and follow-ups.
The team was first established in the region in 2019.
Could this intervention team help villages trust police in northern Quebec?
It expanded over the last couple of years in the shadow of eroding trust between Inuit and the Nunavik Police Service (NPS) — compounded by several high-profile police-involved shootings.

In 2024, communities across the province took part in marches to denounce police brutality in the region after police fatally shot 26-year-old Joshua Papigatuk and injured his twin brother, Garnet, in an incident that made headlines across the province.
Not long after, the family of Mark R. Annanack, who died in Kangiqsualujjuaq, Que., following a fatal police shooting, co-signed a letter calling for changes within the NPS.

items: No charges in fatal police shooting in Kangiqsualujjuaq, Que.

blocks.text: This month, Annanack's father and Papigatuk's surviving twin brother, Garnet, issued a statement to members of the National Assembly, ministers and Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Chief of the Nunavik Police Service, Jean-François Bernier, says public trust is "coming back slowly," but that there's no doubt people ask questions following a fatal intervention. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)
The families are demanding immediate investments for an overhaul of local judicial and policing services.
"Inuit are dying and our dignity suffers," read the release, issued on a Facebook page titled "Justice for Inuit," just days ahead of the two-year anniversary of Joshua Papigatuk's death, on Nov. 4.
On Tuesday, the province's Crown prosecutor's office announced that charges would not be laid against the officers who shot and killed Joshua.
'MIT should be in every village'

Having partnerships with units like the MIT helps build trust between police and the community, says Capt. Mélanie Panneton, in charge of the southeast division for the NPS, who has worked in Nunavik for the past 11 years.
Capt. Mélanie Panneton is in charge of the southeast division for the Nunavik Police Service. She says the MIT can help build trust. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"It helps us focus on another side of policing," she said, sitting in Kuujjuaq's police headquarters, located in the centre of town.
"It's always a learning opportunity," she said. "It's beneficial to put more [of] the focus on de-escalation."
Caroline Simard, the director of youth protection for the Ungava coast, stands by the MIT approach, noting it responds to situations that aren't necessarily a policing matter.
Caroline Simard, the director of youth protection for the Ungava coast, says she sees results in how the unit builds trust with families. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
According to her, "MIT should be in every village, because it's the best way to intervene."
"It's less stressful for family to see MIT coming, just Saqijuq, than [the Department of Youth Protection]," she said.
"There's the image that we're going to take children and send them down south and then family won't ever see their children again."

items: Foster care is modern-day residential school system: Inuk MP Mumilaaq Qaqqaq

blocks.text: Bringing 'softness' and fairy wings
Nunavik police officer Const. Tommy Bertrand Dell'Accio is opening his mind to a new way of doing things.
Here he was, in the backseat of Saqijuq's MIT vehicle earlier this month, holding pink sparkly fairy wings and a matching wand.
The day earlier, he says he wore the accessories after a special request from a young girl the team was assisting.

Nunavik Police officer, Const. Tommy Bertrand Dell'Accio, seen here with Sophie Bergeron, a trainee on the intervention team, held sparkly fairy wings and a matching wand at the request of a young girl the team assisted in November. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
"And now she's actually asking for me to put it back again," he said smiling, during a ride-along with CBC News, on his way to meeting the girl for a second consecutive day.
The streets were dark as the team hurried to help transfer the child to a group home in the northern community, located along Quebec's Ungava Bay.
"I told you I had the wand," said Bertrand Dell'Accio, greeting her alongside Richard and the team's newest trainee, Sophie Bergeron.
He handed the girl a sparkly accessory as a gift and followed her up the group home's steps.
Later, back in the car, he noted despite his being on shift — and in uniform — his role that night was meant as a support.

items: Family of twins shot by Nunavik police call for justice at Montreal protest

blocks.text: "To show the population as well that police officer[s] are not just here to arrest people, but they're here to get involved," he said.
The MIT — when not on call — is focused on prevention and building connections by participating in local events, like karaoke, volleyball or trick-or-treating, says Richard.
Ariane Richard drove the mobile unit's car one evening in November. The unit takes on interventions that require time, sensitivity and follow-ups. (CBC)
"My goal and our goal … is really to bring a little bit of softness and joy even when it's a rough time," she said.
"There's a way to bring … happiness in any of our interventions, and that's really the goal of it."
Trust in Nunavik police was at 'its lowest,' says chief
Confidence in police has historically been lower amongst Indigenous people in Canada, as outlined in a number of Statistics Canada reports.
In the 2020 general social survey, 22 per cent of Indigenous people reported having little or no confidence in the police.
When Nunavik Police Chief Jean-François Bernier first began in the role in 2025, he says confidence in the police was at "its lowest."
"I truly understand why," said Bernier. "People need answers. They need to be closer to their police force. The police force need[s] to be more transparent."
In 2025, CBC reported that the rate of fatal shootings by police officers was roughly 73 times higher in Nunavik than the Quebec average, according to the provincial police watchdog.
Since last year, Bernier says, public trust is "coming back slowly." But he says there's no doubt people ask questions following a fatal intervention.
Nunavik Police Chief Jean-François Bernier says part of his approach to leading the department involves being on the ground and accessible. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)
Even when the Crown prosecutor determines that police acted lawfully, Bernier calls it a "lose-lose situation," that leaves families, communities — and the police service — with deep wounds.
"Because I don't know any police officers who get up in the morning and say, 'Oh, I hope I'll be involved in this serious incident and I'm going to fight for my life today,'" he said.
"It doesn't work that way."
Part of Bernier's approach to leading the department involves being on the ground and accessible, he says, and answering hard questions.

By the end of this year, he noted he will open a new position within his executive office for an Inuk advisor that will report to him. The person's mandate will be to challenge the decisions of the police service.
Rebuilding trust, Bernier says, will take time.
"Once I get the full confidence of the public, and I will," he said. "We're never going to lose the confidence again."
Problems to continue if justice is out of Inuit hands, says elder
But Charlie Watt, an Inuk elder and former Canadian senator, says he's heard that same message many times over his lifetime.
He was one of the negotiators for the 1974 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement.
The agreement was Canada's first modern Indigenous land claims treaty, and signalled a new era for Nunavimmiut to gain more self-governance, including in policing.
Charlie Watt says he is thinking about creating a specialized group of Inuit to start tackling the justice issues. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)
At one point, Watt pushed for the idea of setting up the police force under Inuit control. To this day, however, he says Inuit life continues to be handled by "the outside."
"We don't have our self government in place," he said. "That's our biggest enemy at the moment."
Sitting in his living room, overlooking the Kuujjuaq River, 82-year-old Watt is surrounded by mementos from his life in politics, and photos of family growing up on the other side of the river.
The modern community of Kuujjuaq, now the largest in Nunavik, completely changed over the course of Watt's lifetime.
Kuujjuaq, located along the Ungava Bay, is the largest northern village in the region of Nunavik. (Rachel Watts/CBC)
Reflecting on justice and policing systems in his region, his perspective is that the relationship between police and Inuit never used to be this bad.
"They have [a] tendency to shoot before they open their mouth," he said, pointing to the fact that some officers get training in western Canada, through the RCMP.
"You have to train them where they [are] going to do the work."
He says Inuit also have to take on more responsibility, when it comes to policing their communities.
He is thinking about leveraging his experience to help jumpstart a specialized group of Inuit to start tackling justice issues.
When it comes to long-term solutions to systemic problems, the elder says: "They can only come from the Inuit."

articles.title: Oddly enough, this video game weighs in on Canada's fighter jet options
articles.summary: The gaming industry might not be the first place to look for military procurement advice, but a recently released video game offers a subtle suggestion for what Canada should pick for its new fighter…

image.caption: Gamers play Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve in Chiba, Japan, in September. The game ranks the F-35 ahead of the Gripen-E in its tree of unlockable aircraft. (Kiyoshi Ota/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The gaming industry might not be the first place to look for military procurement advice, but a recently released video game offers a subtle suggestion for what Canada should pick for its new fighter jet fleet.
Ace Combat ranks F-35 above Gripen — both being considered by Ottawa
Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve was released in early October. The series, which produced its first game in 1995, is set in a fictional world but uses real-life jets for players to control.

As players progress through the game, they're able to unlock higher-caliber aircraft. Both the American-made F-35 and Swedish Gripen-E, which the federal government is considering purchasing, are available.
The F-35 is ranked near the top of the game's aircraft tree, ahead of the Gripen.

Andy Lee, a doctoral candidate at the University of Toronto who studies video games and military simulations, said it's "super common" for games to have a system where players unlock new equipment as they progress.
"Tech trees are viewed as one of many ways to maintain retention, so there's something to invest in so that you keep playing beyond just narrative completion," she said.
"You're making choices as you progress through the game, which gives you some sense of personalization as well."
What Canada’s fighter jet decision could mean for NORAD

Lee said it's likely the developers, Bandai Namco, consulted defence experts. But she added that the game is not entirely realistic either — given that the company needs to make it playable for gamers.
"Ace Combat is sort of a flight simulator, but it's an arcade-y one, right? What I mean by that is that it's not beholden to total realism. It's supposed to be fun," she said.

"But for the most part, these developers are knowledgeable and they're not simply going off of their gut. So when they balance things from a gameplay perspective, it is probably weighted in some way based around real-world, technical specifications."

The company has to get permission and licenses to use the manufacturer's product in the game and Lee said that likely includes a fee. CBC News asked Bandai Namco for an interview but didn't receive a response.
An F-35 flies over the Toronto lakeshore during a training session before the start of the 2025 Canadian International Air Show. (Alex Lupul/CBC)
For Dave Perry, a defence analyst and president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, it's not surprising that the game ranked the two jets where it did.
"I think by pretty much all assessments [the F-35] aircraft's got a lot more capability than alternatives on the market, including the Gripen," Perry said.
The Canadian Global Affairs Institute gets sponsorship support from defence contractors including Lockheed Martin, manufacturer of the F-35, and Saab, which makes the Gripen.

The F-35 has distinct advantages in being more compatible with other defence products widely used in the North American defence industry and capabilities that aren't available in the Gripen, Perry said, comparing the two fighters to cellphones to make his point.
"F-35 would be the equivalent of current version flagship smartphones. The Gripens are analogous to a much earlier model," he said.

"It'll still make the calls, you can probably do some texting, some other things. But it doesn't have the full product suite and offerings that the flagship model of iPhone does right now — and it isn't the Apple product that works in the Apple ecosystem."
Weighing Canada’s fighter jet options: F-35 vs Gripen
Data obtained by Radio-Canada earlier this year showed National Defence Department testing of both jets in 2021 put the F-35 far ahead of the Gripen.
Prime Minister Mark Carney paused plans to proceed with a planned order for 88 of F-35s in response to diplomatic and trade tensions with the U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.
Under an agreement announced in 2023, Ottawa already has a firm order for 16 F-35s, and has since started to pay for 14 additional aircraft.

Perry noted that there are likely political considerations going into the government's deliberations. But he said that the Gripen does have some advantages that the F-35 doesn't, specifically that it is easy to maintain or alter depending on mission needs.
A Swedish Gripen fighter being fitted with air-to-air missiles during a training exercise in Iceland. Canada is considering purchasing the Swedish fighter jet. (Murray Brewster/CBC)
"You can change all kinds of things on that aircraft, including an engine, with just a few people and a relatively rudimentary pack of tools," he said of the Gripen.

Sources have previously told Radio-Canada that the government is considering a larger mixed fleet of both jets. Saab has offered to build the new jets in Canada, which could mean thousands of new jobs in the country.

The Carney government announced earlier this year its intention to also purchase six of Saab's GlobalEye surveillance jets that would be used to to monitor the Arctic for missiles, drone attacks or enemy incursions. Sources told CBC News earlier this fall that the air force was concerned the GlobalEye meets only a handful of the military's requirements.

When it comes to the current choice of jet fighters, Lee said the government likely isn't going to look at Ace Combat when making its decision. But she noted that simulation technologies are used by governments for training and considering new equipment.
"The line between actual defence simulating software and commercial video games is sometimes pretty thin," she said.
Perry quipped that the government has been dragging its feet on making a final decision that it might as well consult the new game.

"This most recent review of Canada's fighter purchases has gone on so long that maybe they're actually seeing how video gamers assess this aircraft. They've certainly had enough time to look at every conceivable type of analysis, conventional or not," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.
With files from Daniel LeBlanc and Murray Brewster

articles.title: Theft of trade, tech secrets 'a global issue' extending beyond recent headlines: security CEO
articles.summary: Recent episodes have shone a light on the ongoing threat to companies — and by extension, the wider economy — from efforts to surreptitiously steal information and secrets. These include efforts…

image.caption: Jensen Huang has exited Nvidia after a scandal that revealed he'd had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The drive to steal secrets extends beyond the AI and tech sectors — and beyond borders, according to one expert. (Jeffrey McWhorter/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Recent episodes have shone a light on the ongoing threat to companies — and by extension, the wider economy — from efforts to surreptitiously steal information and secrets. These include efforts involving state or state-linked actors.
Recent episodes illustrate risks companies face from those motivated to steal their secrets
Some of the leading tech companies in the U.S. have been finding out recently that the threat of espionage extends into the corporate realm.

At Nvidia, an alleged Chinese spy had a relationship with the company's top executive, Jensen Huang. The scandal has rocked markets, raised national security concerns and led to Huang's ouster. China has denied trying to entrap him. Congress still has questions.

At OpenAI, a former employee was criminally charged after allegedly planting a listening device in a conference room. FBI Director Kash Patel has said that was done "to secretly capture sensitive communications" about the company's technology. The accused has pleaded not guilty to illegally intercepting communications.

And at Google, a former employee was charged and accused of stealing AI technology from the company. In January, a jury convicted the man of multiple counts of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets — with prosecutors stating the theft had benefitted China. A judge later dismissed the espionage-related counts.

These episodes have shone a light on the ongoing threat to companies — and by extension, the wider economy — from efforts to surreptitiously steal information and secrets. These include efforts involving state or state-linked actors.

In Canada, authorities warn that the risks of these types of actions are increasing at a time when the global economy is becoming more competitive and some of the country's key sectors hold knowledge and insights of interest to hostile actors.
A man walks past an OpenAI booth at a tech summit in San Francisco in September. (Carlos Barria/Reuters)
Yet the drive to steal secrets extends beyond the AI and tech sectors — and beyond borders, warns Don Aviv, the CEO of security firm Interfor International.
"This is a global issue," Aviv told CBC News in an interview.
These events happen when a secret can be surreptitiously obtained that will benefit another party, he said.
A problem for Canada, too

Canada's national intelligence agency, CSIS, has warned that the country is "a target" for states seeking "to acquire sensitive research and technology to advance their own strategic political, economic and military advantage."
In its 2025 public report, the spy agency predicted these threats will increase amid a more competitive global economy, as states jostle for advantages.

items: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang signals willingness to return as CEO

blocks.text: AI is one area of interest for states to target at the moment, but it's not the only one that has their attention, according to Stephanie Carvin, an associate professor at the Norman Paterson School of International Affairs at Carleton University in Ottawa.
"It's not just about AI, it's a whole range of high-level technologies," Carvin, a former national security analyst for CSIS, told CBC Radio's Fresh Air.
"In any kind of high-tech area, which is considered to be a strategic priority, where intellectual property is valuable — these are going to be targets as well," she added.
LISTEN | Stephanie Carvin on the reality of current-day espionage:
Fresh Air14:06What does espionage look like in Canada in 2026?
Ottawa has made defending the economy a top priority of its new national security strategy.

The framework plan says "Canadian workers, firms, and innovators need a secure foundation, free from foreign interference, espionage and economic predation, so their efforts can build a prosperous future for all Canadians."

One measure Ottawa plans to take, according to the strategy, is to strengthen the sharing of intelligence information with the private sector and with research institutions. The government says it will also "build intelligence, counterintelligence and security screening capacity to support these partnerships."
Defending against threats
There are companies, like Aviv's own, which provide training on how to prevent these incidents and defend against them.

In general, Aviv said an effort to prevent the theft of a particular set of knowledge or processes involves conducting an assessment of how valuable that information is, how readily it can be stolen and then determining what can be done to protect it in the long run.
Carleton University's Carvin says companies need to carefully consider the level of access to information that is required for the people in their organizations.
"Who has access to what information? What do they need? Do you have a need-to-know policy?" said Carvin.
"Do you have compartmentalization of information?" Carvin asked, noting that may be a more complicated question in an era in which working with AI may require making use of broad swaths of data.
Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang to appear before U.S. Congress next month

In Canada, AI is on a formal list of technologies that Ottawa considers to be sensitive. These carry concerns about to risk to Canada or its allies if such technologies are transferred to adversaries.
Some major AI companies seem to recognize the threats they are facing, given the interest in their technology and products — and they are beefing up their staffing accordingly.
OpenAI appointed Paul Nakasone, the former director of the U.S. National Security Agency, to its board of directors in 2024.

Over at Anthropic, the company announced the creation of a national security and public sector advisory council last year, which included a former deputy director of the CIA and a former executive director of U.S. Cyber Command.
More broadly, Reuters has reported that chip, tech and AI firms have been hiring former intelligence professionals to help guard their secrets.
"The AI firms have snapped up a lot of security talent," Christopher Falkenberg, the president of the New York-based Insite Risk Management, recently told Reuters.
"There are some very sophisticated people out of government thinking about security for these businesses," said Falkenberg, who's also a former U.S. Secret Service agent.
With files from Reuters and CBC Radio's Fresh Air

articles.summary: Trump shares the supposed highlight of his brief state visit to the Philippines but gives no details. Malacañang says both sides reached an understanding on areas of economic cooperation, but does…

Carlos Barria/Reuters

items: US President Donald Trump announced a significant trade deal with the Philippines during his state visit, describing it as the largest trade agreement between the two nations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – US President Donald Trump on Wednesday, November 18, announced what he described as “the biggest trade deal” between the Philippines and the United States during the final activity of his brief state visit to Manila.
Trump disclosed this in his remarks at the state luncheon in his honor in Malacañang Palace following his bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., but gave no details about the deal.

“We’ve just consummated a trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far and it’s a fair deal for both countries. We’re very happy with it. We didn’t know that was going to take place but it took place very quickly. It’s a magnificent deal for both,” Trump said.

“So today, under the leadership of President Marcos and myself, I’m proud to say that we’re making the alliance between the United States and the Philippines much stronger than it’s ever been before, especially with the consummation of this deal,” he added.

blocks.caption: Trump announces ‘biggest trade deal’ between Philippines, US

blocks.text: Marcos’ office later said both sides reached an understanding on areas of economic cooperation, but made no mention of a trade deal.
Trade representatives of both countries will work closely to translate the commitments into concrete initiatives, it said in a statement.

“I am pleased to announce that we made a new and completely different trade deal with the Philippines, one that will be a true landmark, and, in particular, a deal that will be great for our farmers and those in the business of ‘energy,'” Trump said on Truth Social after his Philippine visit, but gave no further details.
Negotiations on a trade deal between the two allies were not mentioned in any schedules released by either country.
“The US offered for us to diversify our food supply and energy requirements,” said Philippine Ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez.
Asked whether anything was signed, Romualdez said in a text message, “None.”

Marcos, in his luncheon speech, said that the partnership between the two countries are also “building stronger ties in trade, in investment, in energy, in technology, resilient supply chains, education.”
Trump said in his remarks at the start of his bilateral meeting with Marcos that the US is expanding its defense cooperation with the Philippines.

The Philippines and the US are treaty allies through the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty, the core of their ties, signed years after Washington recognized Manila’s independence. The treaty covers possible attacks in the South China Sea.

In December 2025, the US Congress passed the Philippines Enhance Resilience Act, which authorizes allocating $500 million annually in foreign military financing to the Philippines, totaling $2.5 billion by 2030.
Trump also signaled that the US wants deepened collaboration in energy security, particularly nuclear energy. He added that the US may do “something very big” in the civilian nuclear industry.
“And for the Philippines to embrace American technology in its first modern nuclear project would underscore the strength of the important relationship,” he said.

In February, the US announced several initiatives to help the Philippines in integrating nuclear power into its energy mix by 2032. This was two years after the enforcement of a landmark civil nuclear cooperation agreement between the two countries in 2024. (READ: A nuclear Philippines in six years? OECD’s nuclear chief isn’t convinced.)

While the Philippines and the US have been strong allies, this alliance was tested during the administration of Marcos’ predecessor, Rodrigo Duterte, who sought a pivot to China, but this foreign policy direction had since been reset under Marcos.

The years that followed saw an increase in the intensity of military training exercises, as well as the frequency of joint sails in the West Philippine Sea, including near areas that China claims or de-facto controls.
Asked if he was concerned about tensions in the West Philippine Sea, Trump told reporters: “I’m not concerned about that at all, that will be taken care of.”
After the state visit and bilateral meeting, Trump headed to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit. – With reports from Reuters/Rappler.com

articles.title: David Lammy urges Andy Burnham to campaign on rejoining EU at next election
articles.summary:
Former foreign secretary’s intervention comes as prime minister prepares for major UK-EU summit in Brussels

David Lammy has urged Andy Burnham to campaign on a promise to rejoin the EU at…

blocks.text: David Lammy has urged Andy Burnham to campaign on a promise to rejoin the EU at the next election.
The former foreign secretary, who also served as deputy prime minister under Keir Starmer, said the prime minister’s Liverpool conference speech “blew the door wide open” on the issue.

“Burnham’s Labour should go into the next election clear that its intention is to rejoin the EU,” Lammy wrote in the Times. “Forming the next government would give it the mandate to begin formal negotiations.
“Once a deal is agreed, this should be put to the people. Unlike the last referendum, the public should have the opportunity to decide between two clearly defined choices.”
His intervention comes as Burnham prepares for a major UK-EU summit in Brussels amid renewed scrutiny over Britain’s relationship with the bloc.

The prime minister promised in his Labour conference speech in September that he would lay out different options to the country around the time of the November summit. But with the Brussels meeting approaching on Friday, Burnham appeared to prolong the timeline.
In a speech on Monday, he said he would start a discussion with the bloc on options after the summit, before presenting options to the public at a later date.

Pressed on whether reopening the Brexit topic had become toxic, the Labour leader told Sky News on Tuesday: “I’m in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal. That’s what I’m doing this week. We’ll see how it goes. And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU. And I’ll set that out later this year alongside the 10-year plan.
“But I don’t agree with you at all, actually, that it’s a toxic debate.”

He repeated his pledge to stick to the 2024 Labour manifesto’s red lines – which rule out returning to the customs union, single market or free movement – before a general election and that the “British public will be in charge of whatever comes next”.
He denied changing the timeframe he had laid out in September, saying: “I will set out next month what the next phase looks like. And that is exactly what I said at my conference speech.”
Burnham also launched an attack on the former Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson, who alongside David Cameron has cautioned him against returning to the bloc.
He also said the youth guarantee scheme to get young people into work, which has formed part of the reset negotiations with the EU, would only be open to British citizens.

Concerns have been raised that the scheme to be agreed at the summit in Brussels on Friday, which could allow tens of thousands of young Europeans to work temporarily in the UK each year, and vice versa, could cut into new support for young Britons.
The former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn announced his recommendations for how to bring down the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) on Tuesday.

He said British young people should be the priority for hiring, whatever the outcome of the EU deal. The prime minister later told ITV’s Good Morning Britain he was looking to create “priority opportunities” for young people. He was asked if the jobs guarantee scheme, which aims to help 90,000 young people into work by March 2029, would exclude Europeans.

He said: “Yes, because we have a situation at the moment through the youth guarantee where employers receive a payment to take on somebody who’s been long-term unemployed. So that’s the scheme and we can, of course, design that scheme to support young British kids who are not in education, employment or training, and absolutely that will be the way we go forward.”

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Wednesday described the overall security situation throughout the ASEAN Summit 2026 as generally peaceful, with only pockets of "minor disturbances"
"Generally peaceful with some pockets of minor disturbances," PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said at a press briefing.
Co denied allegations of police brutality raised by a group of youth protesters who staged a demonstration in front of Camp Crame earlier Wednesday.
He said authorities allowed the protesters to air their grievances and maintained that no police brutality occurred.
"Kagaya po ng palagi nating sinasabi, wala pong magiging pag-aresto kung walang magiging pag-labag ng batas," Co said.
(Like what we always say, there will be no arrests if there were no violations of the law.)
Asked about reports that around 300 protesters were arrested nationwide, Co said the PNP would still have to verify the figures.
He confirmed, however, that arrests had been made in the Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila and Muntinlupa City with cases already filed against those who were apprehended.
Meanwhile, Co thanked the PNP's partner agencies, members of the media, and the public for their cooperation in ensuring the safe and peaceful conduct of the summit. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial should be more than halfway done, says prosecution
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel estimates that Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team is nearing the end of its presentation, with the impeachment trial set to resume this week.

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 4:19pm
Photo shows the Senate session hall set up as a court for the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, scheduled to start on the afternoon of July 6, 2026.
The Philippine STAR / Ryan Baldemor
MANILA, Philippines — The House prosecution panel estimates that Vice President Sara Duterte's defense team is nearing the end of its presentation, with the impeachment trial set to resume this week.

Rep. Joel Chua (3rd District, Manila) said at a press conference on Wednesday, November 18, that Duterte’s defense team previously requested 30 to 32 trial dates in its pre-trial brief to argue the four articles of impeachment raised against the vice president.
However, as only one article — specifically, the claim that Duterte amassed unexplained wealth — was retained, the defense should be wrapping up its arguments within the next few hearings, Chua said.

“What’s disappointing is that although the trial is ending, there’s still no substance. The meat or core of the Article 2, which is unexplained wealth, still hasn’t been disproven,” he said in a mix of English and Filipino.
Prosecution panel adviser Robert “Ace” Barbers agreed with Chua, saying that using all 30 days requested by the defense would be overstretching the trial.
“Hindi na siguro dapat payagan ‘yon (ng impeachment court) kung wala naman ding ebidensiya o witness sa kanilang ipepresenta na papabulaananan ‘yong alegasyon.”
(They shouldn’t be allowed [to stretch the trial] if no evidence or witness they plan to present will actually refute the allegations.)
Barbers added that the defense may be struggling to find evidence to controvert the prosecution’s case.

The evidence provided by the prosecution, he explained, is hard to contest because the documents, such as Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth, came from the vice president’s camp.
Relevance?

Peers of Duterte and her husband, Manases “Mans” Carpio, were called to the stand last week in connection with the couple’s “unusual banking behavior,” including a meal worth P200,007.29 at a restaurant in Japan and P256,000 worth of shoes in Malaysia.
Barbers questioned the relevance of raising these issues, especially as they did not address the allegations against the vice president.

When viewed alongside claims from Duterte’s camp of threats against the lives of former household staff, the issues function like a “smoke screen” that distorts the nature of the allegations, Barbers said.
Chua likewise questioned the relevance of the witnesses called so far, saying that the five individuals who have testified may have further incriminated the vice president.

After dropping 16 bank officials from its witness list, the defense team intends to summon an anti-money laundering lawyer and three government officials to testify on Cale88 Foods Corp.’s financial records.
The company, a banana chip exporter in which Carpio was listed as a shareholder, reported P150 million in revenue in 2025 despite having only two employees.
The trial will resume at 10 a.m. on Thursday, November 19.

articles.title: Ghana's new $60m presidential jet sparks public outrage
articles.summary: The purchase has sparked outrage over its cost as many Ghanaians struggle with rising cost of living.

blocks.text: Manufactured by French aerospace company Dassault Aviation, the aircraft was delivered to the Ghana Air Force on Monday at a reported cost of $61m.
Parliament approved its purchase last December as part of a broader programme to modernise Ghana's military aviation fleet, which also includes four helicopters from Airbus.
The jet was welcomed with a water salute on Monday, but its arrival triggered criticism online and among opposition politicians over the cost and timing of the purchase.
While in the opposition, Mahama himself opposed buying a new presidential jet, prompting questions about why his administration has now gone head with the purchase.

Opposition MP Samuel Abu Jinapor questioned the government's priorities, saying the expenditure came at a time when many Ghanaians continue to struggle with the cost of living and youth unemployment remained alarmingly high.
"What was unacceptable in opposition cannot suddenly become acceptable in government merely because the occupants of power have changed," Jinapor added.
He accused the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) of hypocrisy, recalling how its senior figures had strongly opposed proposals for a new presidential aircraft when they were in opposition.
Jinapor also called for greater transparency over the procurement process, how the purchase was financed and the government's justification for the expenditure.
The purchase has also prompted sharp criticism on social media, with some users arguing the money could have been spent on more pressing public needs.
"This money can employ over 100,000 nurses and 200,000 teachers," an X user posted.
But the government has rejected the criticism, saying Ghana's economic circumstances have changed considerably since the NDC opposed a similar purchase.
Peter Lanchene Toobu, chairman of parliament's defence committee, said the party had never opposed acquiring a presidential jet in principle.
Its objection, he said, had been on the timing when Ghana was experiencing severe economic difficulties.
"We agreed in principle that we needed to purchase a new presidential jet," he said.
He argued, however, that Ghana could not justify the expenditure at a time when it was seeking a $3bn bailout from the IMF.
"The strength and macroeconomic stability of this country have enhanced our status in the sense that imports have become cheaper, and this is the right time," he added.
Toobu said the government had purchased the aircraft without borrowing, citing a stronger Ghanaian currency and improved economic conditions.
Government spokesperson Kwakye Ofosu also dismissed suggestions that the purchase was a misplaced priority.
He pointed to falling prices of construction materials and lower borrowing costs as evidence of the country's improved economic situation.
"When I was campaigning in 2024, and I was donating cement, it cost 115 cedis (£7.5) a bag. Today, for 80 cedis, you will get a bag of cement," he told JoyNews.
The controversy has also extended to the aircraft's interior, following claims that it has a dedicated bedroom and bathroom.
But Ofosu dismissed claims that the jet had such luxury facilities, saying the president has no intention of "bathing in the air".
"There certainly is no bathroom. President Mahama has no intention of bathing in the air," Ofosu said.
He explained that the jet has reclining seats that can be converted into sleeping arrangements but denied that it has a dedicated bedroom.
The government says the new jet will replace the 16-year-old Falcon 900EX, which has suffered recurring maintenance problems, including corrosion and leakages in its fuel tank.
The older jet was reportedly grounded in France for several months in 2025 while undergoing repairs.
Officials say the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops on international trips and improving the reliability of presidential travel.
Additional reporting by Thomas Naadi in Accra

articles.title: ‘I didn’t notice his body being purple’: Byron Bay doula left newborn to inflate a jumping castle, court hears
articles.summary:
Inquest into deaths of four babies born in free births or at home in northern NSW between 2022 and 2024 hears ‘something was seriously wrong’

  • Get our

blocks.text: Baby DH was born in an inflatable pool, in a candle-lit room in his parents’ home near Byron Bay, with no one medically trained present. There are two very different versions of what happened next.

In the parents’ version, the doula reassured them Baby DH was OK, then left to inflate a jumping castle while their newborn turned purple, became floppy, and struggled to breathe. In the doula’s version, everything seemed OK but she suggested they seek more help if they wanted to.
The New South Wales coroner’s court heard the two competing narratives on Wednesday as part of an ongoing inquest into the deaths of four babies born in free births or home births.
The babies died in NSW’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
Baby DH lived for just over eight hours.
“The evidence will be that from his first minutes of life, [Baby DH] showed signs that something was seriously wrong,” the Lismore courtroom heard.
“His parents saw those signs. They raised them again and again with their doula, who they had engaged to watch for exactly that. Their doula, in this case, was a woman named Amy Lou Smith.
“Each time the parents raised their concerns, they were reassured by Amy Lou. An ambulance was not called until moments before [Baby DH] stopped breathing.”

His father described the baby as floppy after birth. “His colour, his whole body was purple with his hands and feet darker still,” the court heard, and Smith told them some purple in the hands and feet was normal.
“I didn’t notice his body being purple,” Smith told the court.

Told the baby’s colour wasn’t improving, Smith said “as long as his abdomen isn’t purple”, according to evidence from the parents. The mother was shocked. His whole body had been purple all along. His temperature was low, 34.5C. Smith suggested trying to get it up to 37C.
“I believed if they had real concerns, that they would call an ambulance and not be texting a non medically trained doula,” Smith told the court.
Smith, the inquest heard, described his laboured breathing as “cute little noises”. “I didn’t say that,” Smith told the court.
The court heard Smith told the couple Baby DH would have been put on oxygen if he was in hospital. But Smith later told the court she didn’t know what the hospital would have done.

He had strange lumps on his body, and wasn’t feeding. Smith suggested they get the lumps checked out, and warned that babies sometimes take a while to latch on to the breast, according to the parents’ evidence.
The court heard Smith left to set up a jumping castle for her son’s birthday. She sent the couple a picture of the castle later, as they were trying to contact a doctor, the court heard.
Smith told the court the castle was already set up, and the couple was happy for her to leave.
“Everything felt like it was OK,” she said.

Eventually, the parents spoke to the GP they had tried to contact earlier. The GP told them to call triple zero. They did, and did CPR until the paramedics got there. But Baby DH was declared dead at the hospital.
After the father had made the emergency call, Smith also told them to call an ambulance, and sent them instructions on infant CPR.
Throughout the hearing, Smith denied that any of her advice or comments constituted clinical advice.

Neonatologist Dr Paul Evans, the court heard, had found Baby DH had a complex heart defect, one that would have shown up on an X-ray. The baby could have been treated, and a birth plan with proximity to a major hospital and specialist cardiac care prepared, the court heard.
The child’s death was not inevitable, Evans found.

While pregnant, Baby DH’s mother decided to rely on a doula. She first approached a woman the court heard was likely to be Sita Tara Kali, a self-described birth keeper who was also involved in the care of another baby previously mentioned during the inquest. But Kali didn’t feel she could help, so they turned to Smith.
The court heard the couple paid for an online “sovereign birth course” for Smith and was reassured that she had enough experience. They agreed on an emergency plan.
Smith, who became a birth doula in 2020, was quizzed on her experience in court.
She has a degree in fine art and has worked as a social worker and a youth worker.

She told the court she is not medically trained in any way but did an online “full-spectrum doula course”. She learned CPR but was not familiar with how to apply it to a newborn – she denied she had given the parents the impression she was.
She had no training about a newborn’s colour, breathing, or feeding, but she did go to a retreat where she learned about referring a woman to more support if needed.

She had been present at 15 births over four years, nine alongside a midwife, and conceded she didn’t know what a low-risk birth would look like. She had read a couple of books about birthing, but they were more “spiritual”, the court heard.
She agreed that she now believes the best model of care for a home birth is for a clinically trained midwife to work alongside a doula.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: Donald Trump calls Venezuela a US 'new acquisition'
articles.summary: United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday described Venezuela as the country's "new acquisition," drawing attention to Washington's control over the South American nation's energy resources.

blocks.text: Published November 18, 2026 3:46pm
United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday described Venezuela as the country's "new acquisition," drawing attention to Washington's control over the South American nation's energy resources.
"Venezuela, which was our new acquisition," Trump said during a speech ahead of his bilateral talks with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacañang.
"It was an acquisition, whether people like to say that or not. And it's been amazing what's happened to the United States," he added.
Trump made the remarks while discussing the United States' energy supply, making the country supposedly the world's leading producer of oil and natural gas "by a lot."
"We have more energy than any country in the world by double, even more than that. If you add Russia and Saudi Arabia together, we're much bigger than those two combined," he said.
"And then you add Venezuela, which was our new acquisition. It was an acquisition whether people like to say that or not. And it's been amazing what happened to the United States," Trump added.

Trump said the United States was looking to expand its energy exports to allies in the Pacific, including the Philippines, citing a planned major pipeline project in Alaska and the country's vast oil and natural gas reserves.
In January, US forces attacked Venezuela and ousted its longtime President, Nicolás Maduro.
Following what he described as a "successful" overnight military operation, Trump said US forces would remain in Venezuela until a new government was established.

Venezuela has millions of barrels of oil loaded on tankers and stored in storage facilities that it has been unable to ship because of a US blockade on its oil exports imposed by Trump in mid-December 2025.
The blockade was part of Washington's escalating pressure campaign against the Maduro government.
Trump arrived at Malacañang on Wednesday for his state visit to the Philippines.
During his meeting with Marcos, Trump announced that the two countries had secured a "big" trade deal but did not provide further details.
Philippine Ambassador to the United States Jose Manuel Romualdez, meanwhile, said the agreement involved food and energy supplies.
"The US offered for us to diversify our food supply and energy requirements," he said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Democrats win Alaska Senate race two weeks after midterms counting began
articles.summary: Confirmation of Mary Peltola's victory caps of the party's rout of the Republicans in the midterms Senate election.

blocks.text: Democrat Mary Peltola has won Alaska's hard-fought Senate race, completing a sweeping victory for the party in the US upper house in the midterm elections.
The win gives the Democrats a 56th Senate seat following a tumultuous and controversial election in Alaska, which featured alleged spoiler recruitment efforts and unprecedented court battles.
It took two full weeks of counting to call a winner in the 3 November poll due to the logistical challenge of collecting ballots from across the state's remote expanse.
The Democratic win is the ninth Senate seat the party took from Republicans in this year's midterms, giving the party control of the US Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump's presidency.
A historic set of victories nationally also saw the party win back the House of Representatives.
In her victory statement, Peltola said the "status quo in DC is not working for Alaska".
She recalled speaking to "elders in tears about empty fish racks" and to parents in rural Alaska choosing between heating their homes and putting food on the table.

Peltola's campaign had come under fire after the New York Times reported Democrats attempted to recruit a candidate named Daniel J Sullivan, a complete political unknown residing in a small coastal town who shared a name with the state's current US Senator and incumbent, Dan S Sullivan, in an alleged attempt to confuse voters.
After legal challenges, state courts ruled the second Daniel J Sullivan could remain on the ballot, and election officials distinguished them on election materials.
Peltola denied having knowledge of the alleged plot but her campaign swiftly came under fire, and both the justice department and Alaska's Republican governor said they would launch investigations.
The Trump administration then filed a lawsuit attempting to stop the certification of the election results if the incumbent Republican Senator Sullivan lost.
A federal judge, though, dismissed the case, following legal challenges from Alaska election officials as well as the Peltola campaign and voting groups.
Due to Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, voters confused about which Dan Sullivan was the incumbent could simply choose each man as their first and second choice.

If they did so, after the first round of voting was complete, tabulation would re-allocate any votes from the non-incumbent Dan Sullivan - who stood little to no chance of winning - to the US Senator.
Experts told the BBC that this process made it difficult for any potential spoiler candidate to have any impact on the results.
An analysis by BBC Verify found that even if every vote for the other Dan Sullivan had gone to the incumbent, Peltola would still have won.

The seat initially was one of several toss-up races that appeared as a must-win for Democrats if they wanted to gain control of the Senate - but by the time Peltola was called the winner, they had seats to spare.
With 99% of ballots counted, Peltola had slightly more than 50%, while Sullivan trailed on less than 46%.
Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and an ally of Trump, campaigned on his record of delivering energy and military investment for the state.
Peltola promised Alaskans a more independent voice in Washington.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said in her victory statement.
"I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families."

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 2:50pm
US President Donald Trump (L) and Philippines' President Ferdinand Marcos Jr attend a luncheon at Malacanang Palace in Manila on Nov. 18, 2026.
AFP / Mandel Ngan
MANILA, Philippines — United States President Donald Trump said on Wednesday, November 18, the US had concluded a major trade agreement with the Philippines.

“We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far. And it’s a fair deal for both countries,” Trump said at a state luncheon hosted by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacañang Palace. He said the deal had not been expected but “took place very quickly.”
No further details have been given as of posting.

Marcos and US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton confirmed at the start of the bilateral talks today that a deal under Pax Silica, the US-led supply-chain initiative on critical technologies and minerals, would not be signed during Trump's visit.

Tariff situation. Philippine exports have faced an additional 12.5% US tariff since July 24, imposed after Washington said it found the Philippines had not adopted and effectively enforced a ban on imports made with forced labor.
This specific duty replaced a 10% levy imposed after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s earlier reciprocal tariffs. Under those reciprocal tariffs, Manila had been given a 19% rate.
In August, Malacañang said the government was negotiating to bring the rate down to 10%, which is the rate the US charges countries that have adopted or committed to forced-labor import bans.
Trade Secretary Cristina Roque earlier confirmed Manila would raise the topic of tariffs in Wednesday’s talks and disclose the outcome afterward.

Earlier, at the bilateral meeting, Trump said Manila and Washington were “going to probably do something very big” on nuclear energy. He also offered US gas from a planned Alaska pipeline to supply the Philippines.

articles.title: US Democrats flip Alaska Senate seat as Mary Peltola wins race
articles.summary: The US Senate's final outstanding midterm election race has been won by Mary Peltola. She unseats Republican Dan Sullivan after winning 50.1% of the vote.

image.caption: The so-called 'blue tsunami' that saw Democrats sweep to victory across the US has swept across AlaskaImage: Lindsey Wasson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Associated Press has declared Democrat Mary Peltola the winner of Alaska's Senate race after making it just over the 50% mark on first-rank votes.
Alaska was the last outstanding Senate race to be declared in the US midterm elections 2026 and makes it the ninth Republican-held Senate seat to be flipped.
The latest victory means the Democrats now hold a 56-44 majority in the US Senate. The 53-year-old is the first Democratic senator from the state in almost 20 years.
Peltola promises to deliver for 'Alaska's working families'
"As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska's working families," Peltola said in a statement.

"As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said.
Peltola beat Republican Dan Sullivan's 131,844 with 144,302 votes, the victory coming after an update in the vote count pushed her to 50.1% of the votes.
Peltola will now become one of the first two Native American women to ever be elected to the US Senate, where she will join Minnesota Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan.
Alaska's vast geography, remote rural communities and lengthy absentee ballot process contributed to a protracted count, with the Senate race taking over two weeks to produce a winner.
Progress or not? Democrats, Republicans pick new leaders in Congress
Vote siphon allegations

The Alaskan Senate race garnered a high degree of national interest after a New York Times report that aides to Peltola allegedly tried to use a second candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr, in an attempt to siphon votes from the Republican Dan Sullivan.
The Trump administration had approached the courts to block certifying the results in the event of there being a potential mix-up.
The legal bid was dismissed by a federal judge ahead of the election.
"My opponent's campaign is literally focused on misleading Alaskans, lying and cheating," Senator Sullivan told reporters in Anchorage on election day.
Peltola has denied any knowledge of an alleged plot. In any case, the margin of victory was greater than the number of votes won by the challenger Dan Sullivan, at just 4, 760.

The Democrats' majority had already been secured, allowing them to block legislation and begin investigations into members of President Donald Trump's administration, but the Alaska win will likely also have a morale impact on both sides.

articles.title: Fact check: Viral 'Duterte ASEAN vs. BBM ASEAN' post recycles 2019 SEA Games footage
articles.summary: A viral Duterte vs BBM ASEAN hosting comparison has one problem: The footage is from 2019

blocks.text: November 18, 2026 | 2:21pm
Former President Rodrigo Duterte and President Bongbong Marcos.
PCO

MANILA, Philippines — A viral social media post framing a comparison between former President Rodrigo Duterte’s and President Bongbong Marcos’ hosting of the ASEAN summit recycles footage from the 2019 Southeast Asian Games.
The viral Threads post falsely presents 2019 SEA Games footage as Duterte’s ASEAN Summit hosting.
Screenshot taken Nov. 18, 2026, 1:30 p.m.

In a Threads post on November 17, a compilation of clips was presented as footage of the former administration’s hosting of ASEAN leaders under Duterte’s “legacy,” and used to criticize Marcos’ chairship.
The video also features the text “PRRD with 7b budget” and “Duterte ASEAN vs BBM ASEAN.”
The post’s caption said:
"THE PEOPLE REMEMBER. HISTORY DOESN'T LIE. AND NO AMOUNT OF PROPAGANDA CAN CHANGE THAT." ???? Strong, direct, and unapologetic. #DUTERTELEGACY #PROUDFILIPINO
Rating: This is false.
Facts
Every clip included in the post was taken from the 2019 SEA Games opening ceremony, misrepresented as footage from the 2017 ASEAN Summit hosted by the Philippines under Duterte.
The Threads post’s compilation of clips was taken from a 2024 TikTok reel posted by a pro-Duterte account praising the former president's leadership.
The SEAG Network uploaded footage of the 2019 SEA Games opening ceremony at the Philippine Arena on November 30, 2019.
The footage used was sourced from the opening ceremony of the 2019 SEA Games held at the Philippine Arena, uploaded by the SEAG Network on YouTube on November 30, 2019.
The Duterte administration allocated P15.5 billion for the Philippines’ hosting of the ASEAN summit and related activities in 2017, not P7 billion as claimed in the video.
In comparison, the Marcos administration allocated a P22.9-billion budget for the 2026 ASEAN Summit hosted by the country.
Why we fact-checked this
The Philippines turned over the ASEAN chairship to Singapore on November 17, the final day of the bloc's 49th Summit.
Criticism over the P22.9-billion allocation for the 2026 ASEAN chairship prompted Malacañang to clarify that the amount also covers the 48th ASEAN Summit in Cebu in May 2026.
Preparations for the November summit included major infrastructure and venue preparations at the Philippine International Convention Center and World Trade Center in Pasay City.
As of November 18, the Threads post has garnered more than 2,000 likes and 100 reposts.
